title: Nasser nationalises the Suez Canal Company
summary: On 26 July 1956, in a speech in Alexandria, President Gamal Abdel Nasser announced that he had signed a decree nationalising the Suez Canal Company, controlled by British and French interests, and that Egyptian officials were taking over its offices as he spoke. The move came a week after the United States, followed by Britain, withdrew their offer to finance the Aswan High Dam, a decision the State Department's historical account links to Egypt's growing ties with Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union. Nasser said canal tolls would pay for the dam and offered compensation to shareholders. Britain and France began military planning, while the Eisenhower administration pursued conferences and a Suez Canal Users' Association. The dispute led to the secret Sèvres agreement with Israel and the invasion of 29 October.

perspectives.framing: Presented the nationalisation as the recovery of an Egyptian asset built with Egyptian labour, a lawful act of sovereignty with compensation offered, and an answer to Western humiliation over the dam; the anniversary is commemorated as a founding moment of Egyptian independence and Arab nationalism.

Prime Minister Anthony Eden and the French government treated the seizure as a breach of the 1888 Constantinople Convention and a threat to Western oil supplies, likened Nasser to the dictators of the 1930s, and argued that he could not be allowed to 'have his thumb on our windpipe'.

The Eisenhower administration opposed the nationalisation but insisted that force be a last resort, seeking a negotiated international regime for the canal; its historical account stresses the effort to keep its allies from military action.

Viewed the crisis as an opportunity to end the Egyptian blockade of the Straits of Tiran and fedayeen raids, and entered secret coordination with France and Britain that produced the Sèvres protocol in October.

title: Israeli Border Police kill 48 Arab villagers at Kafr Qasim
summary: On 29 October 1956, the first day of the Sinai campaign, the Israel Border Police imposed a wartime curfew on Arab villages along the Jordanian armistice line; the district commander, Issachar Shadmi, moved its start from 9 p.m. to 5 p.m. with little notice. At Kafr Qasim a unit under Lieutenant Gabriel Dahan shot residents returning from work. Forty-eight villagers, including women and children, were killed, according to Israeli official and press accounts; the community counts 49, including an unborn child. Eleven policemen were tried; in 1958 eight were convicted, and Judge Benjamin Halevy ruled that a 'manifestly illegal' order, over which 'a black flag' flies, must be refused. Sentences were reduced and all were released by 1960. Israeli presidents expressed regret in 2007 and 2014, and Isaac Herzog apologised at the village in 2021.

perspectives.framing: Long treated the killings as the crime of individual policemen rather than state policy, censored early reporting, and stressed the trial's 'black flag' doctrine as proof of the rule of law; President Isaac Herzog's 2021 apology at the village memorial used the word 'massacre'.

Commemorate the Kafr Qasim massacre annually as the defining atrocity of the military government imposed on Arab citizens from 1948 to 1966, arguing that the light sentences and the promotion of some officers show impunity, and citing later testimony that the curfew was linked to a plan to push villagers across the border.

Examine the case as a landmark in the law of superior orders and debate whether the shootings were a local excess or connected to contingency plans (such as the 'Mole' plan) for expelling border villages during the war; the Israeli court records were declassified in 2022.

title: Suez Crisis: Israel invades Sinai, Britain and France intervene at the Canal
summary: After Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal Company, Britain, France and Israel secretly agreed at Sèvres on a joint operation. On 29 October Israeli forces invaded Sinai; within days they took Gaza and most of the peninsula, reaching Sharm el-Sheikh. Britain and France issued an ultimatum on 30 October, bombed Egyptian airfields and landed at Port Said and Port Fuad on 5-6 November. Under pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the UN General Assembly, which demanded a ceasefire and created the UN Emergency Force, fighting stopped on 6-7 November. Israel put its dead at 171-172; historians estimate Egyptian military dead at 1,000 to 3,000; British post-war estimates put Egyptian dead at Port Said and Port Fuad at about 750, Egyptian figures for civilians at about 1,000; Britain reported 16 dead and France 10. Anglo-French forces left by 22 December.

perspectives.framing: Calls the war the Sinai Campaign or Operation Kadesh, presenting it as a preventive response to the Egyptian blockade of the Straits of Tiran, fedayeen raids from Gaza and the Soviet-bloc arms build-up; the campaign is remembered as a military success that secured a decade of relative quiet on the Egyptian front.

Describes the 'Tripartite Aggression' as a colonial conspiracy to reverse the nationalisation of the canal and topple Nasser; the popular resistance at Port Said and the forced withdrawal of the invaders are commemorated as a national victory that consolidated Nasser's leadership of Arab nationalism.

Justified intervention at the time as a police action to separate the combatants and safeguard the canal; the collusion with Israel, later documented, and the humiliating withdrawal under American financial pressure are treated in British accounts as the end of Britain's imperial role in the Middle East.

The Eisenhower administration opposed the use of force by its allies and backed General Assembly demands for a ceasefire and withdrawal; the UN presents the crisis as the birth of armed peacekeeping through UNEF I.

location: Khan Yunis and Rafah, Gaza Strip (under Israeli occupation)
title: Killings at Khan Yunis and Rafah during the Israeli occupation of Gaza
summary: During the Israeli occupation of the Gaza Strip that followed the Sinai campaign, Israeli forces conducted screening operations for weapons and fedayeen in the towns and refugee camps. According to a special report by UNRWA director Henry Labouisse to the UN General Assembly in December 1956, the agency received from sources it considered trustworthy lists of 275 people, 140 refugees and 135 residents, allegedly killed at Khan Yunis and its camp on 3 November, the day the town was taken, and recorded 111 dead, 103 of them refugees, in a screening operation at the Rafah camp on 12 November, where Israeli authorities and UNRWA agreed that refugees had been killed and wounded by the occupying forces. Israel did not deny the deaths but said its soldiers had met armed resistance; a UN observer described the treatment of civilians as 'unwarrantedly rough'. Israel withdrew from Gaza in March 1957.

perspectives.framing: The UNRWA director reported the Khan Yunis lists as persons 'allegedly killed' and the Rafah deaths as agreed by both Israeli and agency sources, presenting the episodes as grave incidents affecting refugees under the agency's care during a military occupation.

Stated that its troops met local militants and that a battle broke out at Khan Yunis, and that the Rafah deaths occurred when a crowd disrupted a screening operation; official Israel neither denied the killings nor acknowledged wrongdoing at the time.

Describe the Khan Yunis and Rafah killings as massacres of unarmed men lined up against walls and shot after the fighting had ended, commemorated as among the deadliest episodes of the 1956 occupation and as evidence of collective punishment of the refugee population.

title: Israel withdraws from Sinai and Gaza; UNEF deploys along the armistice line
summary: After the Anglo-French departure in December 1956, Israel held Gaza and the Sharm el-Sheikh area for four more months. In February 1957 the General Assembly called for complete withdrawal, and President Eisenhower publicly warned of UN sanctions. On 1 March Foreign Minister Golda Meir told the Assembly that Israel would withdraw on the basis of stated 'assumptions': that the Straits of Tiran would remain open to Israeli shipping and that UNEF would be stationed in Gaza, backed by American assurances on navigation. Israeli forces left Gaza and, according to the UN, withdrew their last units from Rafah on 8 March. UNEF, about 6,000 troops from ten countries, took up positions along the Egypt-Israel armistice line and at the straits. Egypt reinstated its administration of Gaza within days, and the canal reopened in April.

perspectives.framing: Presented the withdrawal as reluctant compliance obtained through American assurances on free passage through the Straits of Tiran and on preventing fedayeen raids, and later cited the 1957 'assumptions' to argue that Egypt's 1967 closure of the straits was a casus belli; opposition leader Menachem Begin denounced the withdrawal.

Regarded the withdrawal as the completion of Egypt's political victory over the 'Tripartite Aggression', insisted that UNEF was present only with Egyptian consent and on Egyptian territory, and rejected any implication that Israel had acquired rights in Gaza or the Gulf of Aqaba.

Treats UNEF I, proposed by Lester Pearson and organised by Dag Hammarskjold, as the first armed UN peacekeeping force, whose mandate was to secure and supervise the cessation of hostilities and withdrawal, and then to act as a buffer between Egyptian and Israeli forces.

The Eisenhower administration combined public pressure for unconditional withdrawal with private assurances about navigation rights; the State Department's historical account presents the outcome as evidence of American leverage over its allies and of the shift of Western influence in the region to Washington.

title: First Palestinian National Council founds the Palestine Liberation Organization
summary: Following a decision of the first Arab League summit in Cairo in January 1964, which entrusted Ahmad Shuqayri, Palestine's representative at the League, with organising the Palestinian people, the first Palestinian National Council met in Jordanian-ruled East Jerusalem from 28 May to 2 June 1964. Some 400 delegates from Palestinian communities across the Arab world (sources give 397 invited and 422 members) adopted the Palestinian National Charter and a basic law and, on 2 June, proclaimed the Palestine Liberation Organization with Shuqayri as chairman of its executive committee. The charter defined Palestine within its Mandate borders as the homeland of the Palestinian Arab people, called for its liberation, and rejected the Balfour Declaration and the partition of Palestine, while Article 24 disclaimed sovereignty over the West Bank and Gaza to reassure Jordan and Egypt. The Alexandria summit of September 1964 endorsed the organisation and a Palestine Liberation Army.

perspectives.framing: Marks the founding as the re-emergence of the Palestinian people as a political actor after sixteen years of dispersal, the first representative national institution since 1948, and the beginning of the organised struggle for liberation and return; Fatah, founded separately, initially viewed the PLO as an Arab-state creation.

Nasser sponsored the organisation as the collective Arab answer to Israel's diversion of the Jordan River, giving Palestinians a voice under Arab League tutelage while keeping the initiative for war or peace in the hands of the states.

King Hussein permitted the congress in Jerusalem but insisted on the charter's disclaimer of any claim to the West Bank, viewing the PLO as a potential rival for the loyalty of Jordan's Palestinian majority; relations soured within two years.

Regarded the PLO as an instrument of the Arab states committed by its charter to the destruction of Israel, and refused any dealings with it; Israeli material emphasises that the charter was adopted in 1964, before Israel controlled the West Bank or Gaza.

location: Eilabun, Lower Galilee, Israel (National Water Carrier)
title: Fatah's first armed operation targets Israel's National Water Carrier
summary: At dawn on 1 January 1965 a small squad from Fatah, the movement organised in Kuwait by Yasser Arafat, Khalil al-Wazir and Salah Khalaf, attempted to sabotage Israel's National Water Carrier at the Eilabun tunnel in the Galilee; the charge failed. On the way back across the armistice line one member, Ahmad Musa, was shot dead by a Jordanian patrol. The operation, claimed under the name al-Asifa ('the storm'), caused no Israeli casualties but is marked by Fatah as the launch of the Palestinian armed struggle; some accounts date it to 2 or 3 January. It targeted the centrepiece of a water dispute: Israel had completed the carrier in 1964 to pump Jordan River water from Lake Tiberias to the Negev, and the January 1964 Arab summit had adopted a plan to divert the river's headwaters in Syria and Lebanon.

perspectives.framing: Celebrates 1 January 1965 as the 'launch of the revolution' (intilaqa), the moment Palestinians took their cause into their own hands rather than waiting for Arab armies; Fatah describes its fighters as fedayeen and the raids as resistance operations.

Treated the sabotage attempts of 1965-66 as terrorist infiltration sponsored from Syria and passing through Jordan and Lebanon, and answered them with reprisals against those states; Israel defended the carrier as a lawful use of its share of the Jordan waters under the unratified 1955 Johnston Plan.

Jordan tried to suppress Fatah infiltration for fear of Israeli retaliation, while Syria's Ba'athist government sheltered and encouraged the movement while pursuing the Arab League headwater-diversion project.

location: As-Samu, near Hebron, Jordanian-held West Bank
title: Israeli army raid on the West Bank village of Samu
summary: On 13 November 1966 Israel launched its largest military operation since 1956, sending armour, infantry and aircraft against the village of as-Samu, south of Hebron in the Jordanian-held West Bank. Israel said the raid answered a mine explosion two days earlier that had killed three soldiers near the border, attributed to Fatah infiltrators from Jordan. Dozens of houses were demolished, according to the UN Truce Supervision Organization's report to the Security Council. Jordanian army units rushing to the village were engaged and Jordanian and Israeli jets fought overhead. Eighteen Jordanians were killed, 15 soldiers and 3 civilians, and 54 wounded, according to Jordanian figures cited by historians; Israel reported one officer, battalion commander Yoav Shaham, killed and ten wounded. On 25 November the Security Council, in Resolution 228, censured Israel. The raid set off riots against King Hussein in the West Bank.

perspectives.framing: Presented Operation Shredder as a reprisal against a village used as a base for Fatah infiltration and as a warning to Jordan to curb attacks from its territory; Israeli leaders later acknowledged that the operation was larger than intended and damaging to the moderate King Hussein.

Denounced the raid as unprovoked aggression against a state that was actively fighting infiltration, and faced accusations from Palestinians and from Cairo and Damascus that its army had failed to defend the West Bank, prompting martial law and a rupture with the PLO.

The Security Council deplored the loss of life and heavy damage to property, censured Israel for a 'large-scale military action in violation of the United Nations Charter and of the General Armistice Agreement', and warned that repeated reprisals would lead it to consider further and more effective steps.

Widely regard Samu as a milestone on the road to the 1967 war, as it undermined Hussein at home, exposed the absence of an Arab defence pact and contributed to the escalation between Israel and Syria; the Johnson administration voted for the censure and airlifted military equipment to Jordan.

location: Demilitarised zone near Tel Katzir, Israel-Syria armistice line, and skies over the Golan and Damascus
title: Israel-Syria border clash escalates into air battle; six Syrian MiGs shot down
summary: On 7 April 1967 an exchange of fire in the demilitarised zone below the Golan Heights, where Syrian gunners shelled Israeli tractors cultivating disputed land near Tel Katzir, escalated into the largest air battle between Israel and Syria before the June war. Israeli aircraft attacked Syrian gun positions, Syrian MiG-21s rose to intercept them, and in dogfights over the Golan and Damascus Israel shot down six MiGs without loss, according to Israeli accounts cited by the Center for Israel Education and the US State Department; Syria claimed to have downed five Israeli Mirages. Israeli pilots then flew over Damascus. Syria appealed to Egypt under their November 1966 defence pact, and in May Soviet reports of Israeli troop concentrations on the Syrian front, which were false, prompted Nasser's mobilisation in Sinai. Historians widely treat the clash as the opening of the crisis that led to war on 5 June.

perspectives.framing: Described the action as a defensive response to Syrian shelling of farmers in the demilitarised zone and to Syrian sponsorship of Fatah raids, and presented the result as proof of Israeli air superiority; the victory circles over Damascus were intended as a warning.

Held that the demilitarised zones were not Israeli territory and that Israeli cultivation there was a provocation, claimed Israeli aircraft losses, and appealed to Egypt and the Soviet Union for support against what it called an imminent Israeli attack.

Cairo treated the clash as evidence that Israel intended to strike Syria, and Soviet warnings in May of Israeli troop concentrations, later shown to be inaccurate, were used to justify Egypt's deployment into Sinai.

The State Department's historical account and most historians treat the 7 April battle and the Israeli warnings to Damascus that followed as the immediate prelude to the May crisis, while noting US intelligence found no Israeli build-up on the Syrian front.

location: Straits of Tiran, Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt
title: Egypt expels UNEF and closes the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping
summary: In mid-May 1967, after false Soviet reports of Israeli troop concentrations against Syria, Egypt moved large forces into Sinai. On 16 May Egypt asked the UN Emergency Force to leave its border posts, and on 18 May Secretary-General U Thant ordered its withdrawal; UNEF then numbered about 3,400 troops, and 15 of its soldiers were later killed in Gaza when war began. On the night of 22-23 May President Nasser announced from a Sinai airbase that the Straits of Tiran would be closed to Israeli ships and to strategic cargo bound for Eilat. Israel had declared since 1957 that such a blockade would be treated as an act of war. The United States tried unsuccessfully to organise a maritime force to open the straits. Jordan joined Egypt in a defence pact on 30 May, and on 5 June Israel launched the air strikes that opened the Six-Day War.

perspectives.framing: Nasser framed the deployment and the closure as the exercise of sovereign rights over Egyptian territory and territorial waters, the end of an arrangement imposed after the 1956 aggression, and a deterrent against an Israeli attack on Syria; Egyptian statements stressed that Egypt would not fire first.

Described the blockade as an act of war and the removal of UNEF as the collapse of the guarantees on which Israel had withdrawn in 1957; the government of Levi Eshkol and, from 1 June, a national unity cabinet with Moshe Dayan as defence minister presented the June attack as pre-emptive self-defence against encirclement.

U Thant argued that UNEF had been stationed with Egypt's consent and that the Secretary-General had no legal basis to keep it in place once consent was withdrawn, a decision criticised at the time and since, including for bypassing the General Assembly's advisory committee.

The Johnson administration urged Israel not to strike first while it explored an international naval effort (the 'Red Sea Regatta') to open the straits, telling Israel it would 'not be alone unless it decides to go alone'; US intelligence assessed that Egypt was not preparing an offensive.

title: King Hussein signs a mutual defence pact with Egypt in Cairo
summary: On 30 May 1967 King Hussein of Jordan flew to Cairo and signed a mutual defence treaty with President Nasser. The pact declared an armed attack on either state an attack on both and placed Jordanian forces, in the event of war, under the Egyptian chief of staff, General Muhammad Fawzi; Egyptian General Abdul Munim Riad arrived in Amman on 1 June to command the front. The signing was broadcast live on Cairo Radio, and PLO chairman Ahmad Shuqayri, at odds with Hussein since the Samu raid, joined the press conference that followed. Iraq joined the alliance on 4 June. Israeli leaders read the agreement as closing a ring around the country and a sign that Jordan would join any war. When fighting began on 5 June, Jordanian artillery and aircraft attacked Israeli targets despite Israeli messages urging Jordan to stay out.

perspectives.framing: Hussein later explained the pact as an unavoidable response to Arab public opinion and the risk that Jordan would be left isolated or destabilised if it stood aside, and as a means of avoiding the charge of treason that had followed Samu.

Presented the treaty as the completion of a united Arab front that would deter Israel and as proof of Nasser's leadership, with Cairo describing Hussein's arrival as a reconciliation in the face of the enemy.

Cited the pact, alongside the Tiran blockade and the mobilisation in Sinai, as evidence of a coordinated threat on three fronts that justified pre-emptive action; Prime Minister Eshkol broadened his cabinet the next day.

Regard the agreement as the step that brought the West Bank and East Jerusalem into the war, noting that Hussein subordinated his army to an Egyptian command that fed him false reports of victory on 5 June.

location: Allenby (King Hussein) Bridge, Jordan Valley, and the Golan Heights
title: 1967 displacement: hundreds of thousands flee the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan
summary: The June 1967 fighting set off the largest population movement since 1948. As Israeli forces took the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Golan Heights, hundreds of thousands of people crossed the Jordan River or fled toward Damascus, many of them 1948 refugees uprooted a second time. UNRWA's Commissioner-General reported that more than 300,000 people, including about 120,000 registered refugees, were rendered homeless or left their homes in the West Bank and Gaza; other estimates range from roughly 250,000 to 325,000. UNRWA reporting put Syrian movement from the Golan at about 80,000, others say up to 100,000, and an Israeli census in August 1967 found only about 6,400 Syrians remaining. Security Council resolution 237 of 14 June 1967 called on Israel to facilitate the return of those who had fled; Israel permitted only limited returns, and most of the displaced remained in Jordan and Syria. Palestinians call the episode the Naksa.

perspectives.framing: Describes the exodus as a second Nakba or the Naksa, attributing it to Israeli military pressure, the demolition of villages such as Imwas, Yalo and Beit Nuba near Latrun, and the refusal to allow return; the displaced are counted as refugees with a right of return.

Maintained that most people left of their own accord during the fighting or on Jordanian advice, offered a limited family-reunification scheme, and argued that the refugee question could only be settled within an overall peace agreement.

UNRWA registered the newly displaced as 'displaced persons' distinct from 1948 refugees and reported on their numbers; the Security Council and General Assembly called on Israel to facilitate their return.
Holds that the Golan's Arab population was expelled and its villages destroyed, and that the roughly 100,000 displaced and their descendants retain the right to return to the occupied Golan.

location: Three fronts: Sinai, West Bank and Golan (marker at Jerusalem)
title: Six-Day War: Israel defeats Egypt, Jordan and Syria and occupies new territory
summary: On the morning of 5 June 1967, after a May crisis over Egypt's closure of the Straits of Tiran and its build-up in Sinai, Israel launched air strikes that destroyed most of the Egyptian air force and sent its army into Sinai and the Gaza Strip. Jordan opened fire the same day; Israeli forces took East Jerusalem and the West Bank by 7 June and reached the Suez Canal by 8 June. Israel attacked Syrian positions on the Golan Heights from 9 June, and the ceasefire demanded by UN Security Council resolutions 233 to 236 held on all fronts from the evening of 10 June. Israel's Ministry of Defense archive records 776 Israeli dead. No full official Arab toll exists; secondary estimates run to roughly 10,000-15,000 Egyptian, about 700 Jordanian and 1,000-2,500 Syrian soldiers killed. Israel now controlled Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.

perspectives.framing: Presents the war as a pre-emptive act of self-defence against an imminent Arab attack, made unavoidable by the blockade of Eilat, the withdrawal of UN peacekeepers and Nasser's threats; the captured territories are described as security assets and, in the case of Jerusalem, as the reunification of Israel's capital.

Nasser's government initially described the 5 June strikes as aggression carried out with American and British help, a charge it later withdrew; Egypt frames the war as an Israeli attack whose results, the occupation of Arab land, had to be reversed.

Calls the war the Naksa, the 'setback', which placed the whole of Mandate Palestine under Israeli control and created a second wave of refugees, and regards the occupation that began in June 1967 as the central fact of Palestinian life since.

The Security Council confined itself to ceasefire demands during the fighting and then, in resolution 237, called on Israel to facilitate the return of inhabitants who had fled; UN usage refers to the territories taken in 1967 as occupied.

location: East Jerusalem (Old City and surrounding areas)
title: Israel extends its law and administration to East Jerusalem
summary: On 27 June 1967 the Knesset passed three laws enabling the government to extend Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to any area of the former Mandate territory; on 28 June the government applied them to East Jerusalem and about 70 square kilometres of surrounding West Bank land held by Jordan since 1949, and dissolved the Arab municipal council. Israel described the step as municipal unification and denied that it amounted to annexation. The UN General Assembly, in resolution 2253 of 4 July 1967, adopted 99-0 with 20 abstentions including the United States, declared such measures invalid and called on Israel to rescind them; the Security Council reaffirmed this in resolution 252 of 21 May 1968. No state recognised the change. The enlarged municipality became the basis for Israeli neighbourhood construction beyond the 1949 line and remains one of the most contested questions in the conflict.

perspectives.framing: Framed the measures as the reunification of Jerusalem, Israel's eternal capital, guaranteeing free access to holy places of all faiths; it insisted at the time that the laws were administrative rather than an annexation, a position later formalised in the 1980 Basic Law: Jerusalem.

Denounced the annexation of a city it had administered since 1948, retained its claim to the West Bank until 1988 and continued to assert custodianship of the Muslim holy places, including the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount.

The General Assembly and Security Council held that measures changing the status of Jerusalem are invalid, that acquisition of territory by military conquest is inadmissible, and that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.

Regards East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state and describes the expansion of the municipal boundary, land expropriations and residency rules as steps in the city's annexation and Judaisation.

title: Arab summit at Khartoum adopts the 'three noes' resolution
summary: Arab heads of state met in Khartoum from 29 August to 1 September 1967 to coordinate their response to the June defeat. The summit resolution adopted on 1 September pledged to unite Arab political and diplomatic efforts to 'eliminate the effects of the aggression' and secure Israeli withdrawal from occupied Arab land 'within the framework of the main principles to which the Arab states adhere, namely: no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it, and adherence to the rights of the Palestinian people in their country'. It also arranged Saudi, Kuwaiti and Libyan subsidies for Egypt and Jordan and ended the wartime oil embargo. Syria boycotted the meeting and the PLO chairman walked out. American officials read the outcome as a modest step toward realism by Nasser and King Hussein, while Israel cited the 'three noes' as proof that no Arab partner for peace existed.

perspectives.framing: Presented the resolution as a unified rejection of negotiating under occupation and a commitment to recover the occupied territories by political means, while restoring Arab solidarity and financial support for the front-line states.
Cited the 'three noes' for decades as evidence of Arab rejectionism that justified holding the territories pending direct negotiations and a peace treaty.
Officials privately judged that Khartoum marked 'a first short step toward realism', noting the endorsement of political rather than military means and the moderates' influence over the outcome.

Many read the resolution as ambiguous, arguing that Nasser and Hussein used it to legitimise a diplomatic path leading to their acceptance of resolution 242, whereas others see it as confirming Arab refusal of peace.

location: Kfar Etzion, between Bethlehem and Hebron, Israeli-occupied West Bank
title: Kfar Etzion re-established: first Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank
summary: On 27 September 1967 a group of young Israelis, many of them children of kibbutz members killed there in May 1948, re-established Kfar Etzion between Bethlehem and Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, the first civilian Israeli settlement in territory captured in June. Levi Eshkol's government had announced the plan days earlier together with outposts on the Golan and at the northern Dead Sea, describing the sites to the United States as Nahal 'strongpoints' rather than settlements. The move followed the unofficial Allon Plan, drafted by minister Yigal Allon in July 1967, which proposed a line of Israeli settlements along the Jordan Valley and around Jerusalem while returning populated highland areas to Jordan. US diplomats reported by early 1968 that the outposts were becoming permanent civilian kibbutzim. Kfar Etzion began a settlement enterprise that by the 2020s encompassed several hundred thousand Israelis in the West Bank.

perspectives.framing: Described the early sites as security strongpoints in Judea and Samaria and the Golan, and Kfar Etzion specifically as the return of a community destroyed in 1948; later governments refer to settlements as communities and dispute that the Fourth Geneva Convention applies to the West Bank.

Regards settlements as colonies built on confiscated Palestinian land that entrench the occupation and pre-empt a Palestinian state, and points to Kfar Etzion as the start of a deliberate policy rather than a spontaneous return.

Holds that settlements in territory occupied in 1967 have no legal validity and breach the Fourth Geneva Convention, a position later set out in Security Council resolutions 446 (1979) and 2334 (2016).
In 1967-68 Washington privately asked Israel to avoid steps that would appear to prejudge a settlement, and reported that the 'strongpoints' were taking on a permanent civilian character.

title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 242 on 'land for peace'
summary: On 22 November 1967 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted the British-drafted resolution 242, the framework for later Arab-Israeli negotiations. Emphasising 'the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war', it affirmed that a just and lasting peace should include 'withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' and 'termination of all claims or states of belligerency', with respect for every state's right 'to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries'. It also called for freedom of navigation and 'a just settlement of the refugee problem', and provided for a special representative, Gunnar Jarring. Because the English text has no definite article before 'territories', Israel argued that withdrawal need not be total, while Arab states, citing the French text, insisted on full withdrawal. Egypt and Jordan accepted it; Syria rejected it until 1973, and the PLO rejected it as treating Palestinians only as refugees.

perspectives.framing: Reads the resolution as requiring withdrawal only to 'secure and recognized boundaries' negotiated directly with Arab states, not to the 1949 lines, and as linking any withdrawal to peace, an end of belligerency and recognition.

Accepted the resolution as requiring complete Israeli withdrawal from all territories occupied in June 1967 before or as part of any settlement, citing the preamble on the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war and the French text.
Rejected the resolution for two decades because it referred to Palestinians only as a 'refugee problem' and did not recognise their national rights; the PLO accepted it, with 338, in 1988.

As the drafter, Lord Caradon described the wording as deliberately balanced and denied that the missing article was accidental, insisting that the emphasis lay on the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war combined with secure boundaries.

title: Battle of Karameh: Israeli raid into Jordan meets Fatah and Jordanian resistance
summary: Before dawn on 21 March 1968 Israeli forces crossed the Damiya and Allenby bridges into Jordan with armour and air support to attack Fatah bases at Karameh, a Jordan Valley town used for raids into the occupied West Bank, and at Safi south of the Dead Sea. President Johnson's appeal to Eshkol against a reprisal arrived three hours after the operation began. Fatah fighters, joined by Jordanian army artillery and armour, resisted through the day before the Israelis withdrew, having demolished much of the town. Casualty figures are disputed: Israeli figures cite 28 to 33 Israeli soldiers killed, Jordan reported several dozen soldiers dead and Palestinian fighters killed are put at roughly 100 to 200. On 24 March the UN Security Council condemned the 'large-scale and carefully planned' Israeli action in resolution 248. Fatah presented the battle as a victory, and thousands of recruits joined Fatah.

perspectives.framing: Described the operation as a necessary reaction to terrorism after a mine attack on a school bus, aimed at destroying guerrilla bases, and reported that it had localised the fighting and spared civilians.

Fatah calls Karameh (Arabic for 'dignity') the moment the Palestinian resistance stood its ground against the Israeli army, a founding myth that made Yasser Arafat the movement's leader and brought a surge of volunteers.

Credits the Jordanian army's artillery and armour with inflicting the losses that forced the Israeli withdrawal, while the episode also deepened its unease at the fedayeen's growing autonomy on Jordanian soil.
The Security Council deplored the loss of life, condemned the Israeli military action as a violation of the ceasefire and warned that further such acts would lead it to consider more effective steps.

title: Israeli commandos destroy 13 airliners at Beirut airport after Athens attack
summary: On 26 December 1968 two members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine attacked an El Al airliner at Athens airport, killing one Israeli passenger. Holding Lebanon responsible for a group that operated from its territory, Israel retaliated on the night of 28 December: about 45 commandos landed by helicopter at Beirut International Airport and destroyed thirteen Lebanese-owned civilian aircraft in a twenty-minute operation without loss of life. Lebanon, which had stayed out of the 1967 war, protested to the UN Security Council, which on 31 December unanimously adopted resolution 262 condemning Israel for a 'premeditated' attack on a civil airport and holding that Lebanon was entitled to appropriate redress. France, whose helicopters and aircraft were used, tightened its arms embargo on Israel. The raid opened a cycle of Palestinian operations from Lebanon and Israeli reprisals that would dominate the Israel-Lebanon frontier.

perspectives.framing: Justified the raid as a proportionate response to a terrorist attack planned in Beirut, deliberately aimed at property rather than lives, and as a warning to Arab states hosting armed Palestinian groups.

Condemned an unprovoked attack on a neutral country's civil aviation and sought international redress, while facing growing domestic pressure over the Palestinian armed presence that led to the 1969 Cairo Agreement.
The Security Council condemned Israel for a premeditated, large-scale and carefully planned military action against a civil airport and warned of further steps in the event of repetition.
The PFLP claimed the Athens attack as a legitimate operation against Israel's national airline and presented the Beirut raid as proof of Israeli aggression against Arab states.

title: War of Attrition along the Suez Canal ends in a US-brokered standstill ceasefire
summary: After months of intermittent clashes along the Suez Canal, Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser declared early in 1969 that the 1967 ceasefire was void and opened sustained artillery, commando and air attacks intended to make Israel's hold on the east bank of the Canal too costly; the campaign is usually dated from 8 March 1969. Israel replied with air strikes along the Canal and, from January 1970, deep-penetration bombing near Cairo, which led the Soviet Union to send air-defence crews and pilots to Egypt; Israeli and Soviet-flown aircraft fought directly in July 1970. A United States proposal by Secretary of State William Rogers produced a 90-day standstill ceasefire effective at 22:00 GMT on 7 August 1970, later extended. Estimates of the dead vary widely in the secondary literature, from several hundred to more than a thousand Israelis and from about 3,000 to 10,000 Egyptians.

perspectives.framing: Framed the campaign as a war to liberate occupied Sinai by imposing unacceptable losses on Israel, and treated the 1970 ceasefire as a pause that allowed missile batteries to be moved to the Canal in preparation for a crossing.

Described the fighting as Egyptian violations of the ceasefire that justified deep-penetration raids to punish Nasser, and complained that Egypt breached the August 1970 standstill by moving surface-to-air missiles forward.
Saw the war as a dangerous superpower flashpoint after Soviet forces arrived in Egypt, and promoted the Rogers initiative to secure a ceasefire and revive the Jarring mission under resolution 242.

Debate whether the war was an Egyptian failure or a strategic success, noting that Soviet involvement, the missile wall built during the ceasefire and Israeli overconfidence shaped the surprise of October 1973.

title: Black September: Jordan's army fights Palestinian armed groups
summary: Tension between King Hussein and the Palestinian armed organisations based in Jordan peaked after the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine hijacked four airliners on 6 September 1970 and blew up three of them at Dawson's Field near Zarqa. On 16 September the King declared martial law and installed a military cabinet; the next day the army attacked fedayeen positions in Amman and elsewhere. Syrian armoured brigades crossed into northern Jordan on 20 September but withdrew after Jordanian air strikes and Israeli and American threats. On 27 September Hussein and Yasser Arafat signed a ceasefire in Cairo brokered by Nasser, who died the next day. The CIA recorded Arafat claiming more than 7,000 casualties in the Amman camps; later secondary estimates range from about 3,000 to 5,000 dead. Fighting resumed in 1971 until the PLO was expelled to Lebanon; the Black September Organisation took its name from these events.

perspectives.framing: Presents the campaign as the restoration of state authority against armed groups that had created a state within a state, hijacked aircraft on Jordanian soil and threatened the monarchy, and stresses the Syrian invasion as a foreign attack repelled by the army.

Calls the events Black September, a massacre of Palestinian fighters and refugees by a regime acting in concert with Israel and the United States; the expulsion to Lebanon is remembered as a betrayal by an Arab government.
Treated the crisis as a Cold War test, moving the Sixth Fleet and coordinating with Israel to deter Syria, and credited Hussein's victory with averting a wider war.

Justified its incursion as support for the Palestinian resistance under the banner of the Palestine Liberation Army and withdrew amid the refusal of its air force commander, Hafez al-Assad, to commit aircraft.

title: Munich Olympics attack: eleven Israeli team members killed
summary: Early on 5 September 1972 eight members of the Palestinian Black September Organisation entered the Olympic Village in Munich, West Germany, and broke into the Israeli team's quarters, killing wrestling coach Moshe Weinberg and weightlifter Yossef Romano and seizing nine other athletes and officials. They demanded the release of more than 200 prisoners held in Israel; Israel refused, and after a day of negotiation the West German authorities flew the attackers and hostages by helicopter to Fürstenfeldbruck air base, where a rescue attempt collapsed into a gunfight. All nine hostages were killed, along with a West German police officer and five of the attackers; the three surviving attackers were captured and released in October after a Lufthansa hijacking. The Games resumed after a one-day pause. Israel bombed Palestinian bases in Syria and Lebanon within days and began a covert campaign against those it held responsible for the attack.

perspectives.framing: Describes the attack as a terrorist massacre of unarmed athletes, criticises the German rescue operation and the later release of the surviving attackers, and treated the assassination of Black September figures as legitimate counter-terrorism.

Black September, linked to Fatah, presented the operation as an act of the Palestinian resistance intended to free prisoners and force the world to notice the Palestinian cause; the PLO leadership publicly distanced itself from the group by 1974.

Acknowledged the failure of an improvised police operation and the lack of specialist forces, created the GSG 9 counter-terrorism unit, and in 2022 formally apologised and agreed compensation with the victims' families.
Under Avery Brundage the IOC insisted that 'the Games must go on', resuming competition after a memorial service; it has since honoured the victims at later Games.

title: October War (Yom Kippur / Ramadan War): Egypt and Syria attack Israeli forces
summary: At 2 p.m. on 6 October 1973, Yom Kippur and during Ramadan, Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated surprise attack on Israeli forces in occupied Sinai and the Golan Heights. Egyptian troops crossed the Suez Canal and overran the Bar-Lev Line, while Syrian armour broke into the Golan. After heavy initial losses Israel drove Syrian forces back beyond the 1967 line toward Damascus and from 15 October crossed the Canal, encircling Egypt's Third Army; the superpowers airlifted arms to the combatants. The war ended through UN Security Council resolutions 338 (22 October), 339 and 340 (25 October), which created a new UN Emergency Force. Israel's State Archives record about 2,656 Israeli soldiers killed; Golda Meir gave Henry Kissinger a figure of 1,500 to 2,000 dead during the fighting. Egypt and Syria issued no agreed totals; secondary estimates run to roughly 8,000 to 18,500 Arab soldiers killed.

perspectives.framing: Celebrates 6 October as the day the army crossed the Canal and 'restored Arab dignity', treating the war as a victory that broke the post-1967 deadlock and led to the recovery of Sinai; Egyptian accounts play down the later Israeli crossing.

Calls it the Yom Kippur War, a surprise attack that Israel repelled at great cost; the Agranat Commission blamed intelligence and command failures, and the shock reshaped Israeli politics and led to the 1977 change of government.
Presents the October War of Liberation as a coordinated effort to recover the Golan that was undercut when Egypt accepted a ceasefire, and emphasises the return of Quneitra in 1974 as its outcome.

Framed its airlift and diplomacy as preventing an Israeli defeat while avoiding a humiliation of Egypt, and used the outcome to displace Soviet influence in Cairo and launch step-by-step negotiations.

title: Arab oil producers cut output and embargo the United States
summary: On 17 October 1973 Arab oil ministers meeting in Kuwait announced that their states would cut production by 5 per cent at once and by a further 5 per cent each month until Israel withdrew from the territories occupied in 1967 and Palestinian rights were restored. After President Nixon asked Congress on 19 October for 2.2 billion dollars in emergency military aid for Israel, Libya and then, on 20 October, Saudi Arabia announced a complete halt of oil exports to the United States, later extended to the Netherlands and other states. The posted price of Gulf crude roughly quadrupled between October and January. Arab producers lifted the embargo on the United States at a meeting in Vienna on 18 March 1974, after the Egypt-Israel disengagement agreement and American mediation with Syria. The measures caused shortages and recession in importing countries and demonstrated Arab producers' political leverage.

perspectives.framing: Producers presented the cuts and embargo as a legitimate use of Arab resources to support Egypt and Syria and to press the United States and Europe to compel Israeli withdrawal under resolution 242.

Condemned the embargo as blackmail and a threat to the world economy, launched 'Project Independence', and used Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy partly to secure its lifting; the Office of the Historian records the episode as a turning point in US energy policy.
Saw the embargo as evidence that Arab states would use economic warfare against Israel's allies, and worried that Western dependence on Arab oil would erode support for Israel.
Stress that the price rise owed as much to OPEC's unilateral posted-price decisions as to the embargo itself, and debate how far the embargo changed Western policy toward the conflict.

title: UN Security Council Resolution 338 calls for a ceasefire and negotiations
summary: At 12:50 a.m. New York time on 22 October 1973 the UN Security Council adopted resolution 338, a US-Soviet draft negotiated in Moscow by Kissinger and Brezhnev, by 14 votes to none with China not participating. It called on all parties 'to cease all firing and terminate all military activity' within twelve hours in the positions they occupied, called for implementation of resolution 242 'in all of its parts', and decided that negotiations 'between the parties concerned under appropriate auspices' should begin immediately and concurrently with the ceasefire. Egypt and Israel ordered a ceasefire for 18:52 local time, but fighting continued as Israeli forces completed the encirclement of Egypt's Third Army; the Council reaffirmed the ceasefire in resolution 339 on 23 October and created UNEF II in resolution 340 on 25 October. With 242, resolution 338 became the agreed basis for later Arab-Israeli negotiations.

perspectives.framing: Kissinger presented the resolution as a superpower agreement that ended the war on terms preserving Israel's battlefield position while committing the parties, for the first time, to direct negotiations under American auspices.

Accepted the ceasefire to save the Third Army and read the call for negotiations 'under appropriate auspices' as leading to full Israeli withdrawal under 242; Egypt accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by advancing after 22 October.

Accepted the resolution under American pressure, valued its call for negotiations between the parties, and disputed Egyptian claims about the 22 October lines when the Council demanded a return to them.

Accepted 338 only on 23 October and with the understanding that it required Israeli withdrawal from all territories occupied in 1967 and respect for Palestinian rights; this marked Syria's first acceptance of resolution 242.

title: Egypt and Israel sign the Sinai I disengagement agreement at Kilometre 101
summary: On 18 January 1974 the chiefs of staff of Egypt and Israel signed the first disengagement of forces agreement, known as Sinai I, at Kilometre 101 on the Cairo-Suez road, witnessed by UNEF commander General Ensio Siilasvuo. It followed a week of shuttle diplomacy by Henry Kissinger between Aswan and Jerusalem, after the Kilometre 101 military talks and the Geneva Conference of December 1973. Israel agreed to withdraw from the west bank of the Suez Canal and from a strip east of it, Egypt kept a limited force on the east bank, and a UN buffer zone separated the sides, with restricted-armament zones beyond it monitored by UNEF and American aerial reconnaissance. Implementation was completed by early March 1974, allowing Egypt to reopen the Canal in 1975. The agreement ended the siege of Egypt's Third Army and was the first Egypt-Israel accord since the 1949 armistice.

perspectives.framing: President Sadat presented the agreement as the first fruit of the October crossing, restoring Egyptian sovereignty over the east bank of the Canal and opening a diplomatic path, backed by the United States, toward full recovery of Sinai.

Prime Minister Meir's government accepted withdrawal from the Canal in return for the release of the Third Army pressure, prisoner exchanges, limitations on Egyptian forces and an American commitment to Israel's security, describing it as separation of forces rather than a political settlement.
Kissinger treated Sinai I as proof that step-by-step diplomacy under American auspices could produce results where the Geneva framework could not, and as leverage for lifting the Arab oil embargo.
UNEF II supervised the disengagement, manned the buffer zone and inspected the limited-forces zones, reporting to the Security Council under resolution 340.

title: Israel and Syria sign a disengagement agreement; UNDOF created
summary: After 32 days of Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy between Damascus and Jerusalem, and months of artillery duels on the Golan front, Israel and Syria signed an Agreement on Disengagement in the Egyptian-Israeli military working group of the Geneva Conference on 31 May 1974. Israel undertook to withdraw from the salient it had captured in October 1973 and from the town of Quneitra and a narrow strip along the 1967 ceasefire line, which returned to Syrian civil administration; an area of separation patrolled by a new UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF), created the same day by Security Council resolution 350, and equal zones of limited forces and armaments were established on either side. Prisoners of war were exchanged in June. The agreement ended the fighting of the October War on the Syrian front, and UNDOF's mandate has been renewed at six-month intervals ever since.

perspectives.framing: President Assad presented the agreement as recovering Quneitra and the 1973 losses without recognising Israel, insisting it was a military disengagement and only a first step toward full Israeli withdrawal from the Golan; Syria accused Israel of razing Quneitra before handing it over.

Valued the agreement for ending the war of attrition on the Golan, securing the return of Israeli prisoners and obtaining a Syrian commitment against guerrilla attacks from its territory, while retaining the Golan plateau captured in 1967.
Kissinger regarded the accord as his most difficult negotiation, extending step-by-step diplomacy to Israel's most hostile neighbour and enabling the Arab oil embargo to remain lifted.
The Security Council welcomed the agreement as implementing resolution 338 and created UNDOF to supervise the area of separation, an arrangement it has renewed every six months since 1974.

title: Rabat summit names PLO sole Palestinian representative; Arafat addresses UN
summary: At the seventh Arab League summit in Rabat, Morocco, on 28 October 1974, Arab heads of state recognised the Palestine Liberation Organization as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and affirmed its right to establish a national authority on any Palestinian territory that was, in the resolution's wording, liberated. Jordan's King Hussein, whose government had claimed to speak for West Bank Palestinians, accepted the decision. On 13 November 1974 PLO chairman Yasser Arafat became the first representative of a non-state entity to address a plenary session of the UN General Assembly, telling delegates that he carried an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun. On 22 November the Assembly adopted Resolution 3236, affirming Palestinian rights to self-determination, national independence and sovereignty and the right of return, and Resolution 3237, granting the PLO observer status. Israel and the United States voted against both resolutions.

perspectives.framing: Presents Rabat and the UN appearance as international recognition of the Palestinian people as a national actor with the PLO as its sole legitimate representative, and describes the armed struggle as legitimate resistance to occupation; Arafat's speech is remembered for the 'olive branch' formula.

Rejected the PLO as a terrorist organisation committed by its covenant to Israel's destruction, opposed its admission to the General Assembly and regarded Resolution 3236 as one-sided; Israel did not recognise the PLO until 1993.
King Hussein reluctantly accepted the Rabat decision, giving up Jordan's claim to negotiate for the West Bank, while maintaining administrative and legal ties to the territory until 1988.

Describes 1974 as the year the Palestinian question returned to the General Assembly agenda as a question of the inalienable rights of a people rather than solely a refugee problem, with the PLO invited to participate as an observer.

title: Lebanese civil war begins with the Ain al-Rummaneh bus attack in Beirut
summary: On 13 April 1975 gunmen fired on a congregation outside a Maronite church in Beirut's Ain al-Rummaneh district, where Phalangist (Kataeb) leader Pierre Gemayel was attending a service, killing four people. Hours later Phalangist gunmen attacked a bus carrying Palestinians through the same district, killing about 27 passengers according to most accounts, with reported figures ranging from 22 to 30. The killings ignited fighting between Christian militias and an alliance of the PLO and the leftist Lebanese National Movement, beginning a civil war that lasted until 1990. Syrian forces intervened in June 1976 and were later endorsed by the Arab League as an Arab Deterrent Force; Israel armed Christian militias and, from 1978, a client militia in the south. The PLO's armed presence in Lebanon, sanctioned by the 1969 Cairo Agreement, was central to the conflict. Commonly cited estimates put the war's death toll at 120,000 to 150,000.

perspectives.framing: Described the fighting as a defence of Lebanese sovereignty against an armed Palestinian 'state within a state' that had drawn Israeli reprisals onto Lebanon, and portrayed the church shooting as the provocation that began the war.

Called the bus attack the 'Ain al-Rummaneh massacre' and the opening act of a Phalangist campaign against Palestinians and their Lebanese allies, framing the war as a struggle against a sectarian Maronite-dominated order.
Presented its 1976 intervention as restoring order and preventing partition of Lebanon, acting with Arab League endorsement; critics on all sides saw it as an attempt to control Lebanon and the PLO.

Generally treat the 13 April incidents as the trigger rather than the cause of a war rooted in sectarian power-sharing, socioeconomic grievances, the Palestinian armed presence after 1970 and regional rivalries.

title: Land Day: six Palestinian citizens of Israel killed during Galilee strike
summary: On 30 March 1976 Palestinian citizens of Israel held a general strike and demonstrations against a government plan to expropriate roughly 20,000 dunams (about 2,000 hectares) of land in the Galilee, much of it Arab-owned, for state and Jewish development projects. Israeli police and army units entered villages including Sakhnin, Arraba and Deir Hanna to confront protesters; in clashes there and in Kafr Kanna and Taybeh six unarmed Palestinian citizens of Israel were shot dead, about 100 people were injured and hundreds were arrested, according to Palestinian civil-rights organisations and press accounts. The strike was the first mass political mobilisation of Arab citizens of Israel since 1948, and the date has been commemorated annually since then as Land Day (Yawm al-Ard) by Palestinians in Israel, in the occupied territories and in the diaspora. The land expropriation nonetheless proceeded.

perspectives.party: Palestinian citizens of Israel / Palestinian leadership
perspectives.framing: Commemorate Land Day as a founding moment of collective Palestinian identity inside Israel and as resistance to what they call the 'Judaization of the Galilee' and the confiscation of Arab land; the six dead are described as martyrs of the land.

Described the expropriations as lawful development of state land for the whole population, and characterised the strike as illegal disturbances incited by the Communist Party (Rakah) in which security forces responded to violent rioting.

See 1976 as the point at which Arab citizens of Israel, under military government until 1966, began organising as a national minority; the day later became a pan-Palestinian commemoration linking citizens of Israel with the occupied territories.

title: Likud wins Israeli election, ending Labour's dominance; Begin becomes PM
summary: In elections to the ninth Knesset on 17 May 1977 the right-wing Likud bloc led by Menachem Begin won 43 of 120 seats, ahead of the Labour Alignment's 32, ending almost three decades of Labour-led government since 1948 in what Israelis called the mahapach, or upheaval. Begin formed a coalition with the National Religious Party and Agudat Yisrael, appointed Labour's Moshe Dayan as foreign minister and later added the centrist Democratic Movement for Change. The new government was ideologically committed to retaining the West Bank and expanded Israeli settlements there and in the Gaza Strip and the Golan Heights. Under Begin, Israel nonetheless entered negotiations with Egypt that produced the Camp David Accords and the 1979 peace treaty, while confrontation with the PLO in Lebanon led towards the 1982 war.

perspectives.framing: Presented the victory as a democratic revolution ending Labour's hegemony and affirming the Jewish people's right to the whole Land of Israel; Begin described Judea and Samaria as liberated, not occupied, territory.

Viewed Begin, a former Irgun commander, as an advocate of permanent Israeli control of the occupied territories, and pointed to accelerated settlement building as evidence that the autonomy offered at Camp David was not intended to lead to statehood.
The Carter administration initially feared Begin's positions would obstruct a comprehensive settlement, but later worked with him to reach the Egyptian-Israeli agreements.

title: Sadat visits Jerusalem and addresses the Knesset
summary: On 19 November 1977 Egyptian President Anwar Sadat flew to Israel, becoming the first Arab head of state to visit the country, after telling the Egyptian parliament on 9 November that he was ready to go to the ends of the earth, even to the Knesset, in search of peace. Prime Minister Menachem Begin had responded with a formal invitation. On 20 November Sadat addressed the Knesset in Jerusalem, offering peace and recognition in return for Israeli withdrawal from all territories occupied in 1967 and a solution of the Palestinian question based on self-determination; Begin replied that everything was negotiable except Jerusalem. The visit broke the Arab consensus against direct dealings with Israel: Syria, Libya, Algeria, South Yemen and the PLO condemned it and formed a Steadfastness and Confrontation Front. It opened the direct negotiations that led to the Camp David summit of September 1978.

perspectives.framing: Sadat presented the journey as a bold initiative to break the psychological barrier between Arabs and Israelis and recover Sinai, insisting he sought a comprehensive peace including Palestinian rights rather than a separate deal.

Welcomed the visit as historic recognition of Israel by the largest Arab state and as vindication of its call for direct negotiations, while rejecting full withdrawal to the 1967 lines and any Palestinian state.

Condemned the visit as a betrayal of Arab solidarity and of the Palestinian cause, and accused Sadat of pursuing a separate peace that would leave the occupation of the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan intact.
The Carter administration, which had been pursuing a Geneva conference with Soviet participation, shifted to supporting direct Egyptian-Israeli talks and later mediated them.

title: Coastal Road attack, Operation Litani and UN Resolution 425 creating UNIFIL
summary: On 11 March 1978 eleven Fatah militants who had landed by sea north of Tel Aviv hijacked a bus on the coastal highway; in the ensuing fighting with Israeli forces near Herzliya 38 Israelis, including 13 children, were killed and more than 70 wounded, according to the Israeli government, and nine of the attackers died. On 14 March Israel launched Operation Litani, occupying southern Lebanon up to the Litani River to push PLO fighters from the border. Lebanese and Palestinian figures cited by historians put deaths at roughly 1,100 to 2,000, most of them Lebanese and Palestinian civilians, with between 100,000 and 250,000 people displaced; Israel reported about 20 soldiers killed. On 19 March the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 425, calling for Israeli withdrawal and establishing the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL). Israel withdrew by 13 June, handing border positions to the militia of Major Saad Haddad.

perspectives.framing: Calls the bus hijacking the Coastal Road massacre, the deadliest terrorist attack in Israel to that date, and describes Operation Litani as a necessary military response to eliminate PLO bases used to attack northern Israel.

Described the seaborne raid as a commando operation against Israel led by Dalal Mughrabi, and the invasion as collective punishment of Lebanese and Palestinian civilians intended to destroy the Palestinian presence in south Lebanon.
Protested the invasion as a violation of its sovereignty causing mass displacement, and sought Security Council action to secure Israeli withdrawal and restore state authority in the south.

Resolution 425 called for strict respect for Lebanon's territorial integrity and Israel's immediate withdrawal; UNIFIL's mandate was to confirm the withdrawal, restore peace and security and help the Lebanese government regain authority, tasks it describes as obstructed by Israel's hand-over to the Haddad militia.

title: Camp David Accords signed by Sadat, Begin and Carter
summary: After thirteen days of negotiations hosted by US President Jimmy Carter at the presidential retreat of Camp David, Maryland, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin signed two framework agreements at the White House on 17 September 1978. The Framework for the Conclusion of a Peace Treaty between Egypt and Israel provided for full Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, demilitarised zones and normal relations in exchange for peace. The Framework for Peace in the Middle East proposed a five-year transitional period of full autonomy for the inhabitants of the West Bank and Gaza under an elected self-governing authority, with negotiations on final status, and invoked Security Council Resolution 242. Jordan and Palestinian representatives, invited to join, declined, and the autonomy talks later stalled. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize; an Arab summit in Baghdad in November threatened Egypt with sanctions.

perspectives.framing: Presents the accords as a landmark of American mediation that produced the first Arab-Israeli peace and a framework, however incomplete, for resolving the Palestinian question through negotiation under Resolution 242.

Regarded the accords as securing peace with its most powerful neighbour at the price of Sinai while preserving Israeli claims in Judea and Samaria; Begin insisted that autonomy applied to inhabitants, not territory, and did not preclude settlements.

Sadat described the agreements as the path to recovering all of Sinai and as a first step toward comprehensive peace, though Egyptian foreign minister Muhammad Ibrahim Kamil resigned in protest at the weak linkage to Palestinian rights.

Rejected the accords as a separate peace concluded without Palestinian participation, and argued that 'autonomy' amounted to continued occupation; the Baghdad summit resolved to isolate Egypt if it signed a treaty.

title: Egypt and Israel sign peace treaty in Washington
summary: On 26 March 1979 Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin signed the Egypt-Israel peace treaty on the White House lawn, with Jimmy Carter signing as witness, after Carter's visits to Cairo and Jerusalem earlier that month resolved a deadlock over linkage to Palestinian autonomy. The treaty, the first between Israel and an Arab state, ended the state of war that had existed since 1948, committed Israel to withdraw from the Sinai Peninsula in stages over three years, limited forces in defined zones, guaranteed Israeli passage through the Suez Canal and the Strait of Tiran, and provided for full diplomatic and economic relations; ambassadors were exchanged in February 1980. Most Arab states broke relations with Egypt: the Arab League suspended its membership on 27 March 1979 and moved its headquarters from Cairo to Tunis. The PLO and the Steadfastness Front denounced the treaty as a separate peace that abandoned the Palestinians.

perspectives.framing: Hails the treaty as the cornerstone of Israel's security, removing the largest Arab army from the circle of war in exchange for territory, and as a model of land-for-peace with a state that recognised Israel.

Presents the treaty as the recovery of every inch of Egyptian territory through diplomacy and as fulfilment of Sadat's initiative, while stressing that Egypt continued to support Palestinian rights and the autonomy negotiations.
Condemned Egypt for breaking Arab ranks and recognising Israel without a settlement for the Palestinians, Syria or Jordan, and expelled Egypt from Arab institutions until 1989.
Regards the treaty as one of the major achievements of US diplomacy, underwritten by large annual military and economic aid to both countries and by the Multinational Force and Observers in Sinai.

title: Knesset passes Jerusalem Basic Law; Security Council Resolution 478 rejects it
summary: On 30 July 1980 the Knesset enacted the Basic Law: Jerusalem, Capital of Israel, declaring 'Jerusalem, complete and united' to be the capital of Israel and the seat of the president, Knesset, government and Supreme Court. The law consolidated the extension of Israeli law to East Jerusalem carried out in June 1967 and was passed while Egyptian-Israeli talks on Palestinian autonomy were under way, prompting Egypt to suspend them. On 20 August 1980 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 478 by fourteen votes to none, with the United States abstaining, declaring the law null and void, affirming that it violated international law and calling on states with diplomatic missions in Jerusalem to withdraw them. The thirteen countries with embassies in the city subsequently moved them to Tel Aviv. Israel maintains that Jerusalem has been its capital since 1949; Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.

perspectives.framing: Describes the Basic Law as a declaratory affirmation of Jerusalem's status as the eternal, undivided capital of the Jewish people, changing nothing on the ground, and regards Resolution 478 as a political act that ignores Jewish history in the city.

Calls the law the annexation of occupied Arab Jerusalem and a violation of international law, and demands East Jerusalem, including the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount, as the capital of a Palestinian state.

Holds that the acquisition of territory by force is inadmissible, that East Jerusalem is occupied territory, and that measures altering the character and status of the city are null and void; Resolution 478 has been reaffirmed in later resolutions.
Protested that the law violated the spirit of the Camp David framework and suspended the autonomy negotiations in response.

title: Israel applies its law to the Golan Heights; Security Council Resolution 497
summary: On 14 December 1981 the Knesset passed the Golan Heights Law, extending Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to the Syrian territory Israel had occupied since June 1967, in a single-day session called by Prime Minister Menachem Begin. The measure, widely described as annexation, replaced military government with civilian administration and offered Israeli citizenship to the roughly 13,000 Druze residents, most of whom refused it and staged a months-long general strike in 1982. On 17 December 1981 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 497, declaring the Israeli decision null and void and without international legal effect and demanding that it be rescinded. The United States suspended a recently signed strategic cooperation memorandum with Israel in protest. Syria continued to demand the return of the entire plateau to the line of 4 June 1967, and the Golan remained the central issue in later Israeli-Syrian negotiations.

perspectives.framing: Argued that Syria had used the heights to shell Israeli communities before 1967, had rejected peace, and that applying Israeli law regularised the status of a strategically vital area; Israel avoids the word annexation and refers to the Golan as sovereign Israeli territory.
Denounces the law as illegal annexation of occupied Syrian land and insists that no peace is possible without full Israeli withdrawal from the Golan.

Resolution 497 and later General Assembly resolutions treat the Golan as occupied Syrian territory to which the Fourth Geneva Convention applies, and reject the Israeli measure as without legal effect.
Most residents declared loyalty to Syria, refused Israeli citizenship and, in 1982, held a general strike against the imposition of Israeli identity cards.

title: Israel completes withdrawal from Sinai under the peace treaty
summary: On 25 April 1982 Israel completed its withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, three years after signing the peace treaty, returning the final third of the territory to Egypt on schedule despite the assassination of Anwar Sadat in October 1981. Earlier stages had returned El Arish in May 1979 and about two-thirds of the peninsula by January 1980. In the final days Israeli soldiers forcibly removed settlers and nationalist protesters from Yamit and other settlements in north-eastern Sinai, which were then demolished, and handed over airfields, oil installations and Sharm el-Sheikh. Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak reaffirmed the treaty, and a US-led Multinational Force and Observers took up positions to monitor the limited-force zones. Sinai became the first territory captured by Israel in 1967 to be returned to Arab sovereignty. A dispute over the small Taba enclave was settled by arbitration in Egypt's favour in 1988 and 1989.

perspectives.framing: Presented the withdrawal as proof that Israel honours agreements and pays a painful territorial price for peace, while insisting that the Sinai precedent of dismantling settlements did not apply to Judea, Samaria and Gaza.
Celebrated 25 April as Sinai Liberation Day, the complete restoration of Egyptian sovereignty over its territory achieved by Sadat's initiative and confirmed under Mubarak.
Opposed the evacuation of Yamit as the uprooting of Jewish communities and a dangerous precedent; the Movement to Stop the Retreat from Sinai organised the resistance.
Noted that Egypt had regained its land while the autonomy framework for the West Bank and Gaza remained unimplemented and settlement construction accelerated.

title: Israel invades Lebanon (Operation Peace for Galilee) and besieges Beirut
summary: On 6 June 1982, after the Abu Nidal group shot its ambassador in London, Israel invaded Lebanon in an operation it named Peace for Galilee, stating the aim of pushing PLO forces 40 kilometres from the border. Israeli forces advanced far beyond that line, fought Syrian units in the Beqaa Valley, and by 13 June had encircled West Beirut, where the PLO leadership and thousands of fighters were based. The siege lasted until a ceasefire on 12 August. The UN Security Council demanded Israeli withdrawal in Resolution 509 on 6 June. Lebanese police figures cited by news agencies put deaths in Lebanon by late August at about 17,800, most of them civilians; Israel disputed those figures. The IDF reported 368 soldiers killed by the end of the siege. The war ended the PLO's territorial base in Lebanon and drew US Marines into a multinational force.

perspectives.framing: Presented Operation Peace for Galilee as a defensive war to end PLO rocket and terrorist attacks on northern Israel after the July 1981 ceasefire, later expanded by Defence Minister Ariel Sharon to remove the PLO and Syrian forces from Lebanon; Israeli critics called it a war of choice.

Describes the invasion as an attempt to destroy the Palestinian national movement and the refugee camps, and the ten-week defence of Beirut as heroic resistance that ended only when Lebanese allies asked the PLO to leave.

Successive Lebanese governments condemned the invasion and occupation, while Phalangist leaders under Bashir Gemayel welcomed the removal of the PLO and were elected to the presidency in August 1982 with Israeli support.

Resolution 509 demanded that Israel withdraw immediately and unconditionally to Lebanon's internationally recognised boundaries; UNIFIL positions were overrun and the force's mandate could not be carried out.

title: PLO fighters and leadership evacuated from Beirut; Arafat departs for Tunis
summary: Under a plan negotiated by US envoy Philip Habib and accepted by Lebanon, Israel and the PLO, Palestinian fighters began leaving West Beirut on 21 August 1982, supervised by a US, French and Italian multinational force. Yasser Arafat sailed from the port on 30 August and the evacuation ended on 1 September. Contemporary US and press accounts put the number of PLO and Palestine Liberation Army fighters evacuated at roughly 8,000 to 11,000, together with about 3,600 Syrian soldiers; the fighters were dispersed to Tunisia, Syria, Jordan, Iraq, Sudan, the two Yemens and Algeria, and the PLO's headquarters moved to Tunis. The United States gave written assurances that Palestinian civilians remaining in the camps would be protected, and the multinational force left Beirut by 10 September. The departure removed the PLO's last territorial base bordering Israel and left the camps unprotected two weeks before the Sabra and Shatila killings.

perspectives.framing: Presented the departure as an honourable withdrawal after a two-month defence of Beirut, undertaken to spare the city, and accused the United States and Israel of breaking guarantees for the safety of the civilians left behind.

Described the evacuation as the achievement of the war's central aim, the expulsion of the PLO's military infrastructure from Lebanon, and later argued that the PLO's dispersal to Tunis weakened it politically.

Credited the Habib mission with ending the siege without a battle for the city, and framed the multinational force as a short-term guarantor of a peaceful evacuation rather than a peacekeeping presence.

The Lebanese government and most Lebanese factions sought the PLO's departure to end the siege and restore state authority, while Palestinian residents of the camps feared retaliation once the fighters left.

title: Sabra and Shatila massacre in Israeli-controlled West Beirut
summary: Between 16 and 18 September 1982, two days after the assassination of Lebanese President-elect Bashir Gemayel, Lebanese Phalangist (Kataeb) militiamen entered the Sabra neighbourhood and the adjoining Shatila Palestinian refugee camp in West Beirut and killed Palestinian and Lebanese civilians over roughly 36 hours. Israeli forces, which had moved into West Beirut on 15 September, surrounded the camps, allowed the militia in and fired illumination flares at night. Israel's Kahan Commission estimated 700 to 800 dead; Lebanese authorities counted about 460 bodies, and the Palestinian Red Crescent reported more than 2,000, with some estimates higher. The UN Security Council condemned the killings in Resolution 521 on 19 September, and the General Assembly in December termed them an act of genocide. In February 1983 the Kahan Commission found Israel indirectly responsible and Defence Minister Ariel Sharon personally responsible, leading to his resignation; no Phalangist commander was prosecuted.

perspectives.framing: Describes the killings as a massacre of defenceless refugees carried out under Israeli protection after the fighters had left on US guarantees, and holds Israel and its commanders directly responsible alongside the Phalange.

Accepted the Kahan Commission's finding of indirect responsibility for failing to foresee and stop the militia, while stressing that the killings were committed by Lebanese Phalangists and denying that Israeli soldiers took part; some Israelis at the time called the inquiry a model of accountability.
Denied ordering a massacre, portraying the entry into the camps as a search for remaining fighters after Gemayel's assassination; the party has never accepted institutional responsibility.

Resolution 521 condemned 'the criminal massacre of Palestinian civilians in Beirut'; General Assembly resolution 37/123 D of 16 December 1982 resolved that the massacre was an act of genocide, a characterisation contested by Israel and several Western states.
