title: Beirut bombings of 1983 and the emergence of Hezbollah
summary: On 23 October 1983 two truck bombs struck the barracks of the US Marine contingent at Beirut airport and a French paratroop base, killing 241 US service members and 58 French soldiers, according to their governments, along with several Lebanese civilians. Six months earlier, on 18 April 1983, a car bomb had destroyed the US embassy on Beirut's seafront, killing 63 people, including 17 Americans, according to the State Department. A group calling itself Islamic Jihad claimed the attacks; the United States attributed them to Lebanese Shia militants organised with Iranian Revolutionary Guard support, the network that became Hezbollah, which had formed after the 1982 Israeli invasion and published its founding open letter in February 1985. Hezbollah denies responsibility for the 1983 bombings. The multinational force withdrew in February 1984, the Israel-Lebanon agreement of 17 May 1983 collapsed, and Hezbollah's armed campaign against Israeli forces in southern Lebanon began.

perspectives.framing: Describes the barracks bombing as the deadliest terrorist attack on Americans before 2001, attributes it to Hezbollah acting with Iranian direction, and designated Hezbollah a foreign terrorist organisation in 1997.

Presents itself as an Islamic resistance movement born of the 1982 invasion to expel Israeli and Western forces from Lebanon, denies involvement in the 1983 bombings, and describes attacks on foreign troops in Lebanon as resistance to occupation.
Regards Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy created to wage war on Israel from Lebanon, and cites its attacks on Israeli forces from 1983 onward as justification for maintaining the security zone.
Acknowledges supporting the formation of Hezbollah as part of Islamic resistance to Israel and Western intervention, while denying operational responsibility for the Beirut bombings.

title: Israel withdraws to a self-declared 'security zone' in southern Lebanon
summary: Following a cabinet decision of 14 January 1985, Israel withdrew its forces from most of Lebanon in three stages, leaving Sidon in February, the Beqaa and Nabatiyeh areas in April, and completing the pullback on 10 June 1985. It retained a strip roughly 10 to 20 kilometres deep along the border, which it called the security zone, policed together with the South Lebanon Army militia under General Antoine Lahad. The withdrawal, prompted by mounting casualties and domestic opposition, followed the collapse of the 17 May 1983 Israel-Lebanon agreement and a growing guerrilla campaign by Shia militias, including Hezbollah, against the occupation. Israel said the zone was needed to protect its northern towns; Lebanon and the United Nations regarded it as continued occupation contrary to Resolution 425. Fighting between Hezbollah and Israeli and SLA forces continued in and around the zone until Israel's full withdrawal in May 2000.

perspectives.framing: Presented the security zone as a limited defensive buffer to keep attackers away from Israel's northern border after the failure of the 1983 agreement, and the SLA as a local Lebanese partner.
Called the zone an occupation to be ended by resistance, and treated the 1985 withdrawal as the first fruit of its armed campaign; the SLA was described as a collaborationist militia.
The Lebanese government demanded complete Israeli withdrawal under Resolution 425 and did not recognise the SLA, while residents of the zone lived under a mixed Israeli-SLA administration.
UNIFIL reported that Israel's continued control of the zone prevented it from fulfilling its mandate, and the Security Council repeatedly reiterated its call for full withdrawal.

title: Sharon visits Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif; Second Intifada begins
summary: On 28 September 2000, Likud opposition leader Ariel Sharon toured the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif compound in Jerusalem's Old City, escorted by a large Israeli police contingent, to assert Israeli sovereignty over the site after the collapse of the Camp David summit. Palestinian demonstrators clashed with police during the visit, and on 29 September, after Friday prayers, Israeli police used live fire on stone-throwing crowds inside the compound; contemporaneous reports cited by PBS and The Times of Israel put the number of Palestinians killed that day in Jerusalem at up to seven. Protests and armed confrontations spread rapidly across the West Bank, Gaza Strip and, within days, Arab towns inside Israel. It is widely treated as the start of the Second, or Al-Aqsa, Intifada, an uprising lasting roughly until 2005 that, per Encyclopaedia Britannica, produced more than 4,300 deaths at a ratio of roughly three Palestinians to one Israeli.

perspectives.framing: Israeli officials described the visit as a legitimate tour by a member of the Knesset of the holiest site in Judaism and argued that the uprising was premeditated by the Palestinian leadership after the failure of Camp David, using the visit as a pretext; Israel refers to the compound as the Temple Mount and to the uprising as the 'Palestinian terror war' or 'Oslo war'.

Palestinian leaders called the visit a deliberate provocation at Al-Aqsa Mosque, the third-holiest site in Islam, and framed the ensuing 'Al-Aqsa Intifada' as a popular uprising against occupation and the failure of Oslo to deliver a state.

Security Council resolution 1322 of 7 October 2000 deplored the provocation carried out at Al-Haram al-Sharif and condemned the excessive use of force against Palestinians, while calling on Israel to abide by the Fourth Geneva Convention; the Mitchell Committee later found the visit did not cause the uprising but was poorly timed.

title: October 2000 killings of Arab citizens of Israel; Or Commission
summary: Between 1 and 8 October 2000, protests by Palestinian citizens of Israel in Galilee and Triangle towns such as Umm al-Fahm, Nazareth and Sakhnin, held in solidarity with Palestinians in the occupied territories, turned into confrontations with Israeli police. Officers used live ammunition and rubber-coated bullets; per the legal centre Adalah, thirteen unarmed Palestinians were shot dead, twelve of them citizens of Israel and one a resident of Gaza, and hundreds were injured. The government of Ehud Barak appointed a state commission of inquiry under Supreme Court Justice Theodor Or on 8 November 2000. Its report, published on 1 September 2003, found that there had been no justification for the lethal fire, criticised senior police commanders and political leaders, and recommended reforms. No officer was indicted, a point that families and rights groups continue to raise, and the events deepened the estrangement between the state and its Arab minority.

perspectives.framing: The Barak government described the events as violent riots that blocked roads and endangered lives during a national emergency, appointed the Or Commission to examine police conduct, and later accepted its recommendations; Ehud Barak publicly apologised to the families in 2019.

title: Taba talks end without a permanent-status agreement
summary: From 21 to 27 January 2001, Israeli and Palestinian delegations met at the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba in a final attempt to reach a permanent-status agreement before Israel's 6 February election. Israel's team was led by Foreign Minister Shlomo Ben-Ami and included Yossi Beilin and Gilad Sher; the Palestinian team was headed by Ahmed Qurei and included Saeb Erekat, Nabil Shaath and Mohammed Dahlan. Negotiators worked from the parameters President Bill Clinton had presented in December 2000 and discussed territory, Jerusalem, refugees and security. Their joint statement of 27 January said the sides had never been closer to agreement but that time constraints made a deal impossible; EU envoy Miguel Moratinos later recorded the positions in an unofficial paper. Ariel Sharon won the election and did not resume the talks, ending the Oslo-era permanent-status process.

perspectives.framing: The Barak government's negotiators described Taba as evidence of Israel's far-reaching offers; the incoming Sharon government said the talks were held by a caretaker government without a mandate and declared their positions non-binding.

Palestinian negotiators said Taba showed that agreement on borders based on the 1967 lines, Jerusalem and refugees was within reach and argued that Israel's election, not Palestinian rejectionism, ended the process.
EU special envoy Miguel Moratinos compiled a 'non-paper' recording the positions reached, which the EU presented as proof of substantial progress on all core issues.

title: Dolphinarium discotheque suicide bombing in Tel Aviv
summary: On the night of 1 June 2001, a suicide bomber detonated explosives packed with ball bearings among a crowd of young people queuing outside the Dolphinarium discotheque on the Tel Aviv beachfront. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 21 Israelis were killed, most of them teenagers from families that had immigrated from the former Soviet Union, and dozens more were wounded; The Jerusalem Post put the number injured at 132. The bomber, Saeed Hotari from the Jenin area, was affiliated with Hamas, which claimed the attack. It was the deadliest single attack inside Israel since the intifada had begun eight months earlier. Under heavy international pressure, Yasser Arafat announced a unilateral ceasefire the following day and Israel's government held back from a large-scale military response, although the lull proved short-lived.

perspectives.framing: Israel called the bombing a 'massacre' of children by a Hamas terrorist, held the Palestinian Authority responsible for failing to act against armed groups, and cited it in demanding that Arafat arrest militants.
Hamas claimed the bombing as a 'martyrdom operation' by its military wing in retaliation for Israeli killings of Palestinians, framing attacks inside Israel as legitimate resistance to occupation.
Arafat condemned the attack and declared a ceasefire, presenting it as a Palestinian commitment to restore calm while accusing Israel of provoking violence through incursions and closures.

title: Sbarro pizzeria suicide bombing in central Jerusalem
summary: On 9 August 2001, at lunchtime, a suicide bomber detonated a device inside the Sbarro pizzeria at the corner of King George Street and Jaffa Road, one of the busiest intersections in central Jerusalem. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 15 people were killed, including seven children, and about 130 were wounded. Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad both claimed responsibility; the bomber, Izz al-Din al-Masri from the Jenin area, had been guided to the site by Ahlam Tamimi, who was convicted in Israel, released in the 2011 Shalit exchange and later charged in the United States, where two victims held citizenship. Israel responded by seizing Orient House, the PLO's headquarters in East Jerusalem, and stepping up strikes on Palestinian Authority facilities, while the attack hardened international views of the escalating violence and increased pressure on Yasser Arafat to act against armed groups.

perspectives.framing: Israel described the bombing as a terrorist massacre targeting families and children, responded by closing Orient House and other PA institutions in Jerusalem, and cited the attack as proof that the PA was not preventing terrorism.

Hamas's military wing claimed the bombing as retaliation for Israel's targeted killings, including a strike in Nablus days earlier, and framed it as resistance; Tamimi has since described the attack without regret in interviews.
Washington condemned the attack, later listed Tamimi as a wanted terrorist and filed charges in 2017, while also criticising Israel's seizure of Orient House as an escalation.

title: Passover bombing at the Park Hotel, Netanya
summary: On the evening of 27 March 2002, as some 250 guests gathered for the Passover seder in the dining room of the Park Hotel in the coastal city of Netanya, a suicide bomber walked past hotel security and detonated a large explosive device. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 30 people were killed, many of them elderly and including Holocaust survivors, and about 140 were wounded; early reports carried by CNN that night gave a toll of 19. Hamas claimed responsibility and identified the bomber as Abdel-Basset Odeh from Tulkarm. The attack was the deadliest against Israeli civilians of the Second Intifada and came at the end of a month of repeated bombings in Israeli cities. Two days later Israel's cabinet ordered Operation Defensive Shield, the largest West Bank military operation since 1967, and the timing overshadowed the Arab League summit in Beirut.

perspectives.framing: Israel called the attack the 'Passover massacre', a deliberate slaughter of civilians at a religious meal, declared the Palestinian Authority an entity that supports terrorism, and cited the bombing as the trigger for Operation Defensive Shield.
Hamas claimed the bombing as a 'martyrdom operation' by its Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades and presented it as a response to Israeli military operations in the West Bank and Gaza.

The Secretary-General condemned the bombing as a terrorist attack on civilians and, within days, the Security Council adopted resolution 1402 calling for a ceasefire and Israeli withdrawal from Palestinian cities.

title: Arab League summit in Beirut adopts the Arab Peace Initiative
summary: On 28 March 2002, the 14th Arab League summit in Beirut unanimously adopted a peace proposal put forward by Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah. The Arab Peace Initiative offered Israel an end to the Arab-Israeli conflict, a peace agreement and normal relations with all Arab states in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from the territories occupied since June 1967, including the Syrian Golan Heights and remaining Lebanese territory, the establishment of an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, and a just solution to the Palestinian refugee question agreed in accordance with UN General Assembly resolution 194. The summit was overshadowed by the Park Hotel bombing the previous evening and by Yasser Arafat's absence after Israel restricted his travel. Israel's government did not accept the plan, though later Arab summits re-endorsed it and the Quartet's Road Map referenced it.

perspectives.framing: Arab states presented the initiative as a historic collective offer of comprehensive peace and normalisation on the basis of 'land for peace' and international legitimacy, and have repeatedly reaffirmed it as a package rather than a starting point for negotiation.

The Sharon government said the plan was a non-starter because it demanded withdrawal to the 1967 lines and a refugee solution based on resolution 194 before negotiations; later Israeli leaders described elements as positive while rejecting its terms as preconditions.
The PLO endorsed the initiative as the Arab consensus for a two-state settlement on the 1967 lines and has cited it in every subsequent negotiation as the framework for a regional peace.

title: Operation Defensive Shield and the battle of Jenin refugee camp
summary: On 29 March 2002, two days after the Park Hotel bombing, Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield, its largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967. Over the following weeks the IDF entered Ramallah, where Yasser Arafat's Muqata compound was besieged, and Tulkarm, Qalqilya, Bethlehem, Jenin and Nablus, imposing curfews and mass arrests. The most contested fighting took place in the Jenin refugee camp from 3 April, where troops faced booby-trapped alleys and armed groups. The UN Secretary-General's report to the General Assembly (A/ES-10/186, August 2002) found that at least 52 Palestinians, up to half of them possibly civilians, and 23 Israeli soldiers died there, did not substantiate early Palestinian claims of a massacre of hundreds, and documented extensive destruction of the camp. Human Rights Watch counted at least 52 Palestinian dead, including 22 civilians. The Church of the Nativity siege in Bethlehem ended on 10 May 2002.

perspectives.framing: Israel described the operation as a defensive campaign to dismantle the 'terrorist infrastructure' behind the suicide bombings, said Jenin camp was a base for attackers, and rejected massacre allegations as a libel, pointing out that it sent infantry rather than bombing the camp from the air.

Palestinian officials called the operation a reoccupation of Area A in violation of Oslo, described the siege of Arafat as an attempt to topple him, and initially alleged that hundreds had been killed in Jenin, later citing the camp's destruction as a war crime.

Security Council resolutions 1402 and 1403 demanded Israeli withdrawal; a proposed fact-finding team was disbanded after Israel objected, and the Secretary-General's report relied on secondary sources, calling for accountability while giving no support to the massacre claim.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented unlawful killings, use of civilians as human shields and disproportionate destruction in Jenin and Nablus and called for war-crimes investigations, while also condemning Palestinian bombings of Israeli civilians.

title: Israel approves and begins building the West Bank barrier
summary: In June 2002, at the height of the suicide-bombing campaign, Israel's cabinet approved and began building a physical barrier between Israel and the West Bank. The 23 June 2002 decision authorised a first phase running roughly 123 kilometres from the Salem checkpoint near Jenin south to the settlement of Elkana, plus sections north and south of Jerusalem; per UN OCHA, that stage was declared complete in July 2003. Rather than following the 1949 Green Line, the route, later planned at more than 700 kilometres of fences, walls, trenches and patrol roads, looped east to enclose settlements, placing Palestinian villages, farmland and East Jerusalem neighbourhoods on the Israeli side; per OCHA, some 85 percent of the planned route lies inside the West Bank. Israel's government described the barrier as a temporary security measure, while Palestinians and rights groups said it amounted to de facto annexation.

perspectives.framing: Israel calls the barrier the 'security fence' or 'anti-terror fence', a reversible, non-political defensive measure to stop infiltration from Judea and Samaria, and credits it with the sharp fall in suicide bombings after 2003.

Palestinians call it the 'separation wall' or 'apartheid wall', argue that its route inside the West Bank seizes land and water, isolates East Jerusalem and predetermines borders, and sought the ICJ advisory opinion through the UN General Assembly.

B'Tselem, Human Rights Watch and OCHA describe the barrier's humanitarian impact on access to land, services and family life and argue that a route on the Green Line would meet security needs without violating international law.

title: Quartet presents the Road Map for Peace
summary: On 30 April 2003, the Quartet of the United States, European Union, United Nations and Russia formally presented Israel and the Palestinian Authority with 'A Performance-Based Roadmap to a Permanent Two-State Solution'. The document set out three phases: an end to violence, Palestinian institutional reform and an Israeli settlement freeze and withdrawal from areas occupied since September 2000; an interim Palestinian state with provisional borders; and permanent-status negotiations aimed at a final settlement, originally targeted for 2005. Its release followed the appointment of Mahmoud Abbas as the first Palestinian prime minister, a condition pressed by Washington. Israel's cabinet accepted the plan on 25 May 2003 while attaching fourteen reservations, and Prime Ministers Ariel Sharon and Abbas endorsed it with President George W. Bush at Aqaba, Jordan, on 4 June 2003. Implementation stalled within months amid renewed attacks, military operations and Abbas's resignation in September.

perspectives.framing: The Bush administration presented the Road Map as the path to its June 2002 vision of two states, insisting on Palestinian security performance and reform as the first step and on reciprocal Israeli obligations on settlements.

Israel accepted 'the steps set out in the Road Map' subject to fourteen reservations, chiefly that Palestinian action against terrorism precede any Israeli obligation, that the refugee 'right of return' be excluded, and that the Arab Peace Initiative not be a reference.
The PA accepted the plan without reservations, stressed the settlement freeze and the 2005 statehood target, and argued that Israel's reservations and continued incursions emptied it of content.
Security Council resolution 1515 of 19 November 2003 endorsed the Road Map and called on the parties to fulfil their obligations under it.

title: Israeli helicopter strike kills Hamas founder Sheikh Ahmed Yassin
summary: In the early hours of 22 March 2004, missiles fired from Israeli helicopters struck Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, the 67-year-old founder and spiritual leader of Hamas, as he was being wheeled out of a mosque near his home in Gaza City after dawn prayers. Yassin, a quadriplegic, died instantly; according to contemporaneous reports by NPR and Voice of America citing Palestinian sources, between seven and nine other Palestinians, including bodyguards and bystanders, were also killed and more than a dozen wounded. Israel's government said Yassin was directly responsible for planning suicide bombings, while the killing drew condemnation from the UN Secretary-General, the European Union and Arab governments; a Security Council resolution criticising it was vetoed by the United States on 25 March. Hamas named Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi as its Gaza leader; he was killed in a similar strike on 17 April 2004.

perspectives.framing: Prime Minister Ariel Sharon called Yassin 'the mastermind of Palestinian terror' and presented the strike as a targeted killing of a legitimate military target responsible for hundreds of Israeli deaths.

Hamas described Yassin as a martyred spiritual leader assassinated while leaving prayer, vowed revenge, and portrayed the killing as proof that Israel's planned Gaza withdrawal was a retreat under fire.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan condemned the 'extrajudicial killing' as contrary to international law and warned it would fuel further violence; the United States vetoed a draft Council resolution it considered one-sided.

title: ICJ advisory opinion finds the West Bank barrier contrary to international law
summary: On 9 July 2004, the International Court of Justice in The Hague delivered an advisory opinion requested by the UN General Assembly (resolution ES-10/14) on the legal consequences of the barrier Israel was building in the occupied Palestinian territory. By fourteen votes to one, with US judge Thomas Buergenthal dissenting, the Court found that construction of the wall and its associated regime in the West Bank, including in and around East Jerusalem, was contrary to international law; that Israel was obliged to cease construction, dismantle the sections already built and make reparation; and that other states should not recognise the resulting situation. Israel, which had contested the Court's jurisdiction and not argued the merits, rejected the opinion as political, pointing to its own Supreme Court ruling of 30 June 2004 ordering route changes on proportionality grounds. On 20 July 2004 the General Assembly voted 150 to 6 to demand compliance.

perspectives.framing: Israel said the Court lacked jurisdiction over a political dispute, that the opinion ignored Palestinian terrorism and Israel's right of self-defence, and that only Israel's own Supreme Court rulings on the fence would be binding; it continued construction along a modified route.

The PLO hailed the opinion as a historic legal victory confirming that the 'wall' and the settlements it protects are illegal, and has cited it in later UN resolutions and international-law initiatives.

Washington argued the Court should have declined the case, said the barrier issue belonged in political negotiations under the Road Map, and voted against the General Assembly resolution endorsing the opinion.
The General Assembly endorsed the opinion in resolution ES-10/15 and later established a register of damage caused by the barrier; the Secretary-General reported that Israel had not complied.

title: Death of Yasser Arafat
summary: Yasser Arafat, chairman of the PLO and president of the Palestinian Authority, died on 11 November 2004 at the Percy military hospital in Clamart, near Paris, at the age of 75. He had fallen ill in mid-October at his Muqata headquarters in Ramallah, where Israel had confined him since 2002, and was flown to France on 29 October; French doctors reported a blood disorder but no definitive cause was made public, which fed enduring, unproven poisoning claims and later Swiss, Russian and French investigations. After a military funeral in Cairo, his body was flown to Ramallah and buried in the Muqata on 12 November amid huge crowds. Mahmoud Abbas succeeded him as PLO chairman the same day, Rawhi Fattouh became interim PA president, and Abbas won the presidential election of 9 January 2005, opening a new phase in Israeli-Palestinian diplomacy.

perspectives.framing: Palestinians mourned Arafat as the symbol of their national movement and 'the father of the Palestinian people'; many officials and the public suspect he was poisoned, and the PA later commissioned forensic tests on his remains.

Israeli leaders called Arafat an arch-terrorist and an obstacle to peace, refused burial in Jerusalem, and said his passing could open the way to a more moderate Palestinian leadership; Israel denies any role in his death.
The Bush administration, which had refused to deal with Arafat since 2002, expressed condolences and framed the succession as an opportunity for reform, democracy and renewed Road Map diplomacy.

title: Sharm el-Sheikh summit: Sharon and Abbas declare a cessation of violence
summary: On 8 February 2005, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and King Abdullah II of Jordan hosted Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon and newly elected Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas at Sharm el-Sheikh, the first such summit in more than four years. In separate closing statements both leaders declared an end to all violence against each other's peoples; Israel undertook to release about 900 prisoners and to hand security responsibility for several West Bank cities back to the PA, and both reaffirmed the Road Map. Hamas and Islamic Jihad said they were not bound by the understanding, and attacks continued at a reduced level. The summit is widely treated as the end of the Second Intifada. Per B'Tselem, Israeli forces killed 6,371 Palestinians and Palestinians killed 1,083 Israelis between September 2000 and September 2010, figures that include Operation Cast Lead; UN OCHA counted 5,848 conflict deaths from September 2000 to August 2007.

perspectives.framing: Sharon presented the declaration as a chance to end the 'terror war' provided the PA dismantled armed groups, and tied prisoner releases and city handovers to Palestinian security performance ahead of the Gaza disengagement.
Abbas framed the summit as a mutual ceasefire and a return to negotiations, and pursued a separate 'calm' (tahdiya) with Hamas and Islamic Jihad in Cairo in March 2005 rather than a crackdown.

Hamas said it was not party to the Sharm el-Sheikh understandings, described them as a unilateral Palestinian Authority commitment, and conditioned any calm on Israeli reciprocity and prisoner releases.
Egypt, with Jordan, cast itself as guarantor of the understandings, returned its ambassador to Israel and prepared to deploy border guards along the Gaza frontier as part of the coming disengagement.

title: Israel evacuates Gaza settlements and withdraws its forces
summary: Between 15 August and 12 September 2005, Israel unilaterally evacuated all 21 of its settlements in the Gaza Strip and four small settlements in the northern West Bank under Prime Minister Ariel Sharon's disengagement plan, which the Knesset had approved in October 2004. Per Encyclopaedia Britannica, some 8,500 to 9,000 settlers lived in Gaza alongside about 1.3 million Palestinians; most left by the 15 August deadline and the rest were removed by soldiers and police in a week of emotional but largely non-violent confrontations, completed on 22 August. Settler homes were demolished, and the last Israeli soldiers withdrew from the Strip on 12 September, ending 38 years of military presence inside Gaza. Israel retained control of Gaza's airspace, coastline and most crossings, and Egypt deployed border guards along the Philadelphi corridor; the United Nations continued to regard the Gaza Strip as occupied territory.

perspectives.framing: Sharon presented disengagement as a painful but necessary unilateral step to improve security and Israel's demographic and diplomatic position, and Israel maintains that its occupation of Gaza ended with the withdrawal; settlers and the religious right condemned it as an 'expulsion' of Jews from their communities.

The PA welcomed the evacuation as the fruit of Palestinian steadfastness but objected that it was unilateral, left Israel in control of Gaza's borders, sea and airspace, and was designed, in the words of Sharon's adviser Dov Weisglass, to put the peace process 'in formaldehyde'.
Hamas claimed the withdrawal as a victory of armed resistance, comparing it to Israel's 2000 exit from Lebanon, and used the claim in its 2006 election campaign.
The UN welcomed the withdrawal as a step under the Road Map while stating that, given Israel's continued control of access, Gaza remained occupied territory under international humanitarian law.

title: Hamas wins the Palestinian Legislative Council election
summary: On 25 January 2006, Palestinians in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem voted for a new Palestinian Legislative Council in the first parliamentary election since 1996. Final results announced on 29 January gave Hamas, running as the Change and Reform list, 74 of 132 seats and the ruling Fatah movement 45, on turnout of roughly 77 percent; international observers judged the vote free and fair. Hamas, which had boycotted the 1996 poll and remained committed to armed struggle, formed a government under Ismail Haniyeh in March 2006. The Quartet responded by demanding that any Palestinian government recognise Israel, renounce violence and accept previous agreements; when Hamas refused, the United States and European Union suspended direct aid and Israel withheld tax revenues it collected for the PA, deepening a financial and political crisis that fed the later Hamas-Fatah confrontation.

perspectives.framing: Hamas presented its victory as a democratic mandate to end Fatah's corruption and to pursue 'resistance' alongside governance, and rejected the Quartet's conditions as an attempt to overturn the election result.

Israel said it would not negotiate with a government led by a terrorist organisation sworn to its destruction, suspended the transfer of Palestinian tax revenues, and treated the PA as a hostile entity until Hamas met the Quartet's conditions.
Washington, which had pressed for the election, said Hamas could not have 'one foot in politics and the other in terror', cut direct assistance to the PA and led the Quartet's three conditions.

The UN, as a Quartet member, endorsed the three principles while urging that humanitarian aid continue; UN officials briefed the Security Council that the outcome created deep uncertainty for the peace process.

title: Cross-border raid from Gaza captures Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit
summary: Before dawn on 25 June 2006, Palestinian militants emerged from a tunnel dug some 300 metres under the Gaza border fence and attacked an Israeli army post near the Kerem Shalom crossing. Per the IDF, two soldiers, Lieutenant Hanan Barak and Staff Sergeant Pavel Slutsker, were killed and several wounded; two attackers also died. Corporal Gilad Shalit, a 19-year-old tank crewman, was wounded and carried into the Gaza Strip. Hamas's armed wing, together with the Popular Resistance Committees and the Army of Islam, claimed the raid and demanded the release of Palestinian prisoners. Israel responded on 28 June with Operation Summer Rains, sending ground forces back into Gaza for the first time since the disengagement and arresting dozens of Hamas legislators and ministers in the West Bank. Shalit was held incommunicado for more than five years until his release on 18 October 2011 in exchange for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners.

perspectives.framing: Israel called the raid a kidnapping and an act of war by the Hamas-led PA, held the Hamas government responsible, and framed Operation Summer Rains as necessary to recover the 'abducted soldier' and stop rocket fire.

Hamas's Qassam Brigades described the operation as a legitimate military action against soldiers and Shalit as a prisoner of war to be exchanged for the thousands of Palestinians held in Israeli jails.

Groups such as Human Rights Watch said Shalit's incommunicado detention without Red Cross access was unlawful, while criticising Israel's collective measures in Gaza, including strikes on the power station, as disproportionate.

title: 2006 Lebanon War between Israel and Hezbollah; UNSC resolution 1701
summary: On 12 July 2006, Hezbollah fighters crossed the Blue Line into northern Israel, killed three soldiers and captured two, Ehud Goldwasser and Eldad Regev; five more soldiers died in a failed rescue. Israel answered with a 34-day air, naval and ground campaign across Lebanon, including Beirut's southern suburbs and a push toward the Litani River, while Hezbollah fired around 4,000 rockets into northern Israel. Per Human Rights Watch, at least 1,109 people were killed in Lebanon, mostly civilians, 4,399 were injured and about one million displaced; per Encyclopaedia Britannica, about 120 Israeli soldiers and more than 40 Israeli civilians were killed. The UN Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 1701 on 11 August, calling for a cessation of hostilities, effective 14 August, an Israeli withdrawal, and an expanded UNIFIL alongside the Lebanese army south of the Litani. Israel completed its withdrawal, except from Ghajar, on 1 October 2006.

perspectives.framing: Israel called the campaign the 'Second Lebanon War', a war of self-defence against an Iranian-backed terrorist organisation that had attacked from sovereign Lebanese territory, and blamed Hezbollah's use of villages for civilian deaths; the Winograd Commission later criticised the war's conduct.

Hezbollah described the raid as an operation to free Lebanese prisoners and the war as a 'divine victory' of resistance against Israeli aggression, claiming to have withstood the IDF and deterred future attacks.

The Siniora government said it had not authorised Hezbollah's raid, condemned Israel's bombardment of Lebanese infrastructure as collective punishment, and sought the ceasefire and international force established under resolution 1701.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented indiscriminate Israeli strikes and cluster-munition use in the war's final days, and Hezbollah's indiscriminate rocket fire on Israeli towns, characterising violations by both sides as possible war crimes.

title: Hamas takes control of the Gaza Strip; Abbas forms emergency government
summary: After months of factional clashes and the collapse of the Mecca unity government, fighting between Hamas and Fatah forces in the Gaza Strip escalated on 7 June 2007 into a week-long battle. By 14 June, Hamas's armed wing and its Executive Force had overrun the Palestinian Authority's security headquarters, the Preventive Security compound and President Mahmoud Abbas's Gaza offices, and Fatah's command structure in the territory collapsed. Per Human Rights Watch, 161 Palestinians were killed in the June fighting, including 41 civilians; Arab News later cited 188 dead and more than 650 wounded. Abbas dismissed Prime Minister Ismail Haniyeh's government on 14 June, declared a state of emergency and appointed Salam Fayyad to lead an emergency cabinet in Ramallah; Hamas rejected the decree. The split left two rival administrations, Hamas in Gaza and the PA in the West Bank, while Israel and Egypt tightened the closure of Gaza's crossings.

perspectives.framing: Hamas called its action a pre-emptive move against a US-backed Fatah 'coup' plotted by security chief Mohammed Dahlan, said it was defending the elected government, and described the outcome as 'liberating' Gaza from collaborators.

Abbas and Fatah described the takeover as a bloody military coup by 'putschists' against Palestinian legitimacy, dissolved the unity government and refused any dialogue with Hamas until it reversed the seizure.
Israel declared Gaza a 'hostile territory' in September 2007, restricted the passage of goods and people, and said it would work with the Fayyad government in the West Bank while isolating Hamas.

The UN Special Coordinator briefed the Security Council on the violent insurrection, mourned two UN staff killed on 13 June, recognised the Fayyad emergency government, and warned of a humanitarian crisis as crossings closed.

title: Israel declares Gaza 'hostile territory' and tightens the blockade
summary: On 19 September 2007, three months after Hamas seized control of the Gaza Strip from Fatah, Israel's Security Cabinet unanimously declared Gaza a 'hostile territory' and announced that it would restrict the passage of goods, reduce fuel and electricity supplies and limit the movement of people, citing continued rocket fire on southern Israel. The decision formalised and tightened the closure that Israel and Egypt had applied to Gaza's crossings since June 2007, with Israel controlling the land crossings, airspace and coastline and Egypt controlling the Rafah crossing. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and Human Rights Watch said cutting essential services to the civilian population would breach Israel's obligations under international humanitarian law, while the United States said it shared Israel's assessment of Hamas. The blockade shaped Gaza's economy and humanitarian conditions for the rest of the era.

perspectives.framing: Framed the decision as a lawful response to Hamas, described as a terrorist organisation that had turned Gaza into hostile territory, and said sanctions would be applied only after legal and humanitarian review so as not to create a humanitarian crisis.
Called the declaration a 'declaration of war' and collective punishment of 1.5 million Palestinians, and said it would not change its policies.

The Secretary-General urged Israel to reconsider, saying any cut-off of vital services would be contrary to Israel's obligations towards the civilian population under international humanitarian and human rights law; UN agencies later described the closure as a blockade amounting to collective punishment.

Human Rights Watch said that cutting fuel and electricity to civilians would violate the laws of war, and rejected the argument that the designation released Israel from its obligations as the power controlling Gaza's borders.

title: Annapolis Conference relaunches Israeli-Palestinian negotiations
summary: On 27 November 2007, US President George W. Bush hosted Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas at the United States Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, with delegations from more than 40 countries and organisations, including Saudi Arabia and Syria. Olmert and Abbas issued a Joint Understanding committing both sides to immediate and continuous bilateral negotiations intended to conclude a peace treaty resolving all core issues before the end of 2008, and to implement their obligations under the 2003 Roadmap, with the United States monitoring compliance. Hamas, which controlled Gaza and was not invited, rejected the conference and staged counter-rallies. Negotiations continued through 2008, including far-reaching Israeli proposals, but produced no agreement before Olmert's resignation and the outbreak of the Gaza war in December 2008.

perspectives.framing: Presented Annapolis as the launch of the first serious final-status negotiations in seven years and as international backing for a two-state solution, with the Roadmap as the framework and the US as judge of compliance.
Olmert described the conference as an opportunity to reach a historic agreement and stressed that implementation of any treaty would depend on Palestinian fulfilment of Roadmap security obligations.
Abbas called for an end to the occupation that began in 1967, a halt to settlement expansion and a resolution of the refugee question, and hoped for a treaty within a year.
Denounced the conference as a betrayal of Palestinian rights, said Abbas had no mandate to negotiate concessions, and organised mass protests in Gaza.

title: Operation Cast Lead: Israel's three-week war in Gaza
summary: On 27 December 2008, after the collapse of a six-month Egyptian-brokered truce and renewed rocket fire from Gaza, Israel launched Operation Cast Lead with air strikes across the Gaza Strip, followed by a ground invasion on 3 January 2009. Israel declared a unilateral ceasefire on 18 January 2009 and Hamas announced its own ceasefire hours later; Israeli forces withdrew within days. Casualty figures diverge. B'Tselem recorded 1,387 Palestinians killed, of whom 773 did not take part in hostilities, including 320 minors, while the Israeli military counted 1,166 Palestinian dead, classifying 709 as combatants and 295 as civilians. Thirteen Israelis were killed, per Amnesty International and the Israeli government: three civilians and ten soldiers, four of them by friendly fire. Thousands of homes were destroyed and the blockade remained in place.

perspectives.framing: Described the operation as a defensive campaign to stop years of rocket and mortar fire on southern Israel and to degrade Hamas's terrorist infrastructure, blaming Hamas for civilian deaths by fighting from within populated areas.
Called the offensive a massacre and aggression against a besieged people, claimed victory for having withstood the assault, and framed its rocket fire as resistance to occupation and blockade.

B'Tselem, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch documented large numbers of civilian deaths, the use of white phosphorus and destruction of civilian property, and called for independent investigations of both Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups.

UN OCHA described a humanitarian crisis compounded by the blockade; the Secretary-General condemned strikes on UN facilities and rocket fire on Israel, and the Human Rights Council established the Goldstone fact-finding mission.

title: Goldstone Report on the Gaza conflict released
summary: On 15 September 2009, the United Nations Fact-Finding Mission on the Gaza Conflict, chaired by South African judge Richard Goldstone and established by the Human Rights Council in April 2009, released its 575-page report on the hostilities of December 2008 to January 2009. It concluded that there was evidence that Israeli forces had committed serious violations of international humanitarian law amounting to war crimes and possibly crimes against humanity, and that rocket and mortar fire by Palestinian armed groups on southern Israel also amounted to war crimes and possibly crimes against humanity. Israel had declined to cooperate with the mission. The report recommended that both sides conduct credible independent investigations within six months and that the Security Council otherwise refer the situation to the International Criminal Court. The Human Rights Council endorsed the report in October 2009 over Israeli and US objections.

perspectives.framing: The mission and the Human Rights Council presented the report as an impartial inquiry into violations by all parties and a step against impunity; the Council endorsed its recommendations and later referred it to the General Assembly.

Rejected the report as biased, born of a one-sided mandate from a Council hostile to Israel, and argued that it ignored Hamas's use of civilians as shields and Israel's right to self-defence; Israel refused to cooperate and conducted its own military investigations.
Welcomed the findings against Israel while rejecting the conclusion that its rocket fire constituted war crimes, describing its actions as legitimate resistance.
Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International urged Israel and Hamas to implement the recommendations and criticised the United States and European states for undermining follow-up.

title: Israeli raid on the Gaza flotilla: nine killed aboard the Mavi Marmara
summary: In the early hours of 31 May 2010, Israeli naval commandos boarded six vessels of a Turkish-led 'Freedom Flotilla' attempting to break the naval blockade of Gaza, about 72 nautical miles from the coast in international waters. On the largest ship, the Mavi Marmara, passengers fought the boarding party and soldiers opened fire; nine activists, eight Turkish citizens and one Turkish-American, were killed and a tenth died of his wounds in 2014. Several Israeli soldiers were injured. Turkey recalled its ambassador and relations with Israel collapsed. A UN Human Rights Council fact-finding mission called the interception unlawful, while the UN Secretary-General's Palmer panel in 2011 found the naval blockade a legitimate security measure but the force used 'excessive and unreasonable'. Israel apologised to Turkey in March 2013 and agreed compensation in 2016; the blockade remained in force.

perspectives.framing: Said the blockade was a lawful measure to stop weapons reaching Hamas, that the flotilla had refused offers to unload aid at Ashdod, and that soldiers fired in self-defence after being attacked with clubs and knives; the Turkel Commission found the raid and blockade legal.
Condemned the raid as state terrorism and piracy in international waters, demanded an apology, compensation and an end to the blockade, and downgraded diplomatic relations.

The Human Rights Council mission found the use of force clearly unlawful and described some deaths as summary executions; the Palmer panel found the blockade lawful but the boarding excessive, and the Secretary-General called for a credible investigation.
Described the activists as martyrs of the siege and the raid as proof of the blockade's brutality, and called on the international community to end it.

title: Gilad Shalit freed in exchange for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners
summary: On 18 October 2011, Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, captured by Hamas-led militants in a cross-border raid near Kerem Shalom in June 2006 and held in Gaza for more than five years, was transferred through Egypt to Israel under an agreement mediated by Egypt and Germany and signed in Cairo a week earlier. In exchange Israel released 1,027 Palestinian prisoners in two phases: 477 on the day of the exchange, sent to Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem or exile abroad, and 550 in December 2011. Those freed included prisoners serving life sentences for attacks that killed Israelis, among them Yahya Sinwar, who later led Hamas in Gaza. Large celebrations were held in Gaza and the West Bank, while in Israel the deal was welcomed by Shalit's supporters and criticised by bereaved families and some security officials.

perspectives.framing: Prime Minister Netanyahu presented the deal as fulfilling the state's duty to bring a captured soldier home, while acknowledging the heavy price of freeing prisoners with 'blood on their hands'.
Celebrated the exchange as a victory for resistance that freed heroes of the Palestinian struggle, and said it proved that capturing soldiers was the way to free prisoners.
Abbas welcomed the freed prisoners in Ramallah, while Fatah figures noted that the deal strengthened Hamas politically at the Authority's expense.
Presented its mediation as evidence of its continuing central role in Palestinian-Israeli affairs after the fall of Mubarak.

title: Operation Pillar of Defense: eight days of Gaza-Israel fighting
summary: On 14 November 2012, Israel opened Operation Pillar of Defense with an air strike that killed Ahmed Jabari, head of Hamas's military wing, after weeks of escalating rocket and mortar fire from Gaza and Israeli strikes. Over eight days Israel struck about 1,500 targets in Gaza, while Palestinian armed groups fired roughly 1,500 rockets at Israel, for the first time reaching the Tel Aviv and Jerusalem areas; the newly deployed Iron Dome system intercepted many. According to B'Tselem, 167 Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces, and six Israelis, four civilians and two members of the security forces, were killed by rocket and mortar fire. An Egyptian-brokered ceasefire, announced in Cairo with US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton present, took effect on 21 November 2012 and included understandings on easing restrictions at Gaza's crossings and along its perimeter.

perspectives.framing: Described the operation as a response to hundreds of rockets fired at Israeli civilians, aimed at restoring deterrence and destroying Hamas's long-range rocket capabilities, and credited Iron Dome with limiting casualties.

Called Jabari's killing an assassination and the operation aggression against Gaza, claimed victory for reaching Tel Aviv and Jerusalem with rockets, and framed the ceasefire terms on crossings as a gain of the resistance.
President Morsi's government condemned Israeli strikes, recalled its ambassador, and presented its mediation of the ceasefire as evidence of Egypt's regional leadership.

B'Tselem reported that most uninvolved Palestinian fatalities occurred in the last four days and questioned the legality of several strikes, while also condemning rocket fire at Israeli civilians as a war crime.

title: UN General Assembly grants Palestine non-member observer state status
summary: On 29 November 2012, the 65th anniversary of the 1947 partition resolution, the UN General Assembly adopted resolution 67/19 by 138 votes to 9, with 41 abstentions, upgrading Palestine from 'observer entity' to 'non-member observer State'. The resolution reaffirmed the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and independence in a State of Palestine on the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, and urged the resumption of negotiations toward a two-state solution. Israel, the United States, Canada and six other states voted against. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas presented the bid in person. Israel responded within days by advancing settlement plans, including in the E1 area east of Jerusalem, and by withholding tax revenues collected on behalf of the Palestinian Authority. The new status enabled Palestine to accede to international treaties and, in 2015, to the International Criminal Court.

perspectives.framing: Abbas called the vote a 'birth certificate' for the State of Palestine and a last chance to save the two-state solution, stressing that it did not replace negotiations.

Prime Minister Netanyahu dismissed the resolution as a meaningless unilateral step that would not change anything on the ground, argued that only direct negotiations could create a Palestinian state, and criticised Abbas's speech as incitement.
Ambassador Susan Rice called the resolution 'unfortunate and counterproductive', saying it placed further obstacles in the path to peace and did not create a state.
The Secretary-General said the vote underscored the urgency of resuming meaningful negotiations, and the Secretariat subsequently used the designation 'State of Palestine' in UN documents.

title: Operation Protective Edge: the 50-day Gaza war
summary: Following the kidnapping and killing of three Israeli teenagers in the West Bank in June 2014, mass arrests of Hamas members and intensified rocket fire from Gaza, Israel launched Operation Protective Edge on 8 July 2014 with air strikes, adding a ground offensive on 17 July aimed at Hamas's cross-border tunnels. Fighting lasted 50 days until an open-ended Egyptian-brokered ceasefire on 26 August 2014. Per UN OCHA, 2,251 Palestinians were killed, including 1,462 civilians, of them 551 children; B'Tselem counted 2,202 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces, 1,391 of whom did not take part in hostilities; an Israeli government report counted 2,125 dead and identified at least 936 as militants. On the Israeli side, 67 soldiers and 6 civilians were killed. About 500,000 Gazans were displaced at the peak and roughly 18,000 housing units were destroyed or severely damaged, per OCHA.

perspectives.framing: Framed the war as self-defence against thousands of rockets and attack tunnels, said Hamas bore responsibility for civilian deaths by embedding in residential areas and using UN facilities, and published its own legal report disputing UN civilian-casualty ratios.

Described the war as steadfast resistance to aggression and siege, claimed the tunnels and rockets had imposed a strategic balance, and demanded an end to the blockade and a seaport as ceasefire terms.

OCHA documented unprecedented destruction and displacement; the Secretary-General condemned strikes on UNRWA schools sheltering civilians and rocket fire on Israel; a Human Rights Council commission of inquiry found possible war crimes by both sides.
Presented itself as the indispensable mediator and blamed Hamas for rejecting its initial ceasefire proposal in mid-July, while keeping the Rafah crossing largely closed.

title: Palestine becomes a State Party to the International Criminal Court
summary: On 1 April 2015, the Rome Statute entered into force for the State of Palestine, making it the 123rd State Party to the International Criminal Court; the Court marked the occasion with a welcoming ceremony at its seat in The Hague attended by Palestinian Foreign Minister Riad al-Malki. Palestine had deposited its instrument of accession with the UN Secretary-General on 2 January 2015, days after a Palestinian statehood resolution failed in the Security Council, and lodged a declaration accepting the Court's jurisdiction retroactively from 13 June 2014, covering the 2014 Gaza war. The Prosecutor opened a preliminary examination in January 2015 and a formal investigation into the situation in Palestine in March 2021. Israel, which is not a State Party, and the United States rejected the accession, arguing that Palestine is not a state, and Israel froze tax transfers to the Palestinian Authority in response.

perspectives.framing: Presented accession as a peaceful, legal path to accountability for Israeli settlement construction and military operations, and as an attribute of statehood following the 2012 UN vote.

Condemned the move as a cynical politicisation of the Court, said Palestine did not meet the criteria of statehood, warned that it exposed Palestinian leaders to prosecution for terrorism, and withheld tax revenues.
Opposed the accession as counterproductive to peace and as an action against Israel, and later imposed sanctions on ICC officials investigating the situation.
The Secretary-General, as depositary, accepted the accession and the ICC welcomed Palestine as a State Party committed to the rule of law.

title: Wave of stabbing, shooting and vehicle-ramming attacks begins
summary: From early October 2015, a wave of largely unorganised attacks by young Palestinians using knives, vehicles and occasionally firearms spread from Jerusalem across the West Bank and Israel, following weeks of tension over access to the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif. An attack near the Lions' Gate in Jerusalem's Old City on 3 October 2015, in which two Israelis were killed, is widely cited as its start. UN OCHA recorded 23 Palestinians killed in the week of 6-12 October alone, the highest weekly toll in the West Bank and Israel since its records began in 2005, with more than 2,300 Palestinians and 32 Israelis injured. Over the following months, according to figures reported by France 24, 34 Israelis and nearly 200 Palestinians, most of them assailants, were killed. Israel added checkpoints, demolished attackers' homes and deployed more troops; the violence gradually subsided during 2016.

perspectives.framing: Described the attacks as a wave of terror driven by Palestinian incitement, including false claims that Israel intended to change the status quo on the Temple Mount, and defended the use of lethal force against attackers.
Attributed the violence to despair under occupation, settlement expansion and provocations at al-Aqsa, accused Israel of 'field executions' of suspects, and called the period a popular uprising.
Praised the attackers as heroes of an 'al-Quds intifada' and called for escalation.

B'Tselem and Amnesty International condemned the attacks on civilians while documenting cases in which Palestinian suspects were shot when they no longer posed a threat, and criticised punitive home demolitions as collective punishment.

title: UN Security Council adopts resolution 2334 on Israeli settlements
summary: On 23 December 2016, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 2334 by 14 votes to none, with the United States abstaining rather than exercising its veto in the final weeks of the Obama administration. The resolution reaffirmed that Israel's establishment of settlements in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, has no legal validity and constitutes a flagrant violation of international law and a major obstacle to a two-state solution; it demanded that Israel cease all settlement activity and called on states to distinguish between the territory of Israel and the occupied territories in their dealings. It also condemned violence and incitement against civilians on all sides. It was the Council's first resolution on settlements since 1980. Israel rejected it, recalled ambassadors from several sponsoring states and accused the US of colluding in its passage; the Palestinian leadership welcomed it as a legal foundation for future action.

perspectives.framing: Prime Minister Netanyahu called the resolution shameful and anti-Israel, said Israel would not abide by it, described the settlements as communities in Judea and Samaria whose status should be settled only by negotiation, and accused the Obama administration of orchestrating the vote.
Welcomed the resolution as a victory for international law and a rebuke to settlement expansion, and cited it in subsequent diplomatic and legal initiatives.

The Obama administration abstained, saying settlements endangered the two-state solution, while stressing that it had not drafted the text; the incoming Trump administration and Congress condemned the abstention.
The Secretary-General welcomed the resolution and instructed the Secretariat to report on its implementation every three months, making it a recurring item on the Council's agenda.

title: United States recognises Jerusalem as Israel's capital
summary: On 6 December 2017, US President Donald Trump signed a proclamation formally recognising Jerusalem as the capital of Israel and directing the State Department to begin relocating the US embassy from Tel Aviv, reversing decades of US policy that the city's status should be settled in negotiations. The proclamation stated that the United States was not taking a position on final-status issues, including the specific boundaries of Israeli sovereignty in Jerusalem. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the decision historic and courageous. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas said the United States had disqualified itself as a mediator, and Palestinian factions called days of protest in the West Bank and Gaza. Arab and Muslim states, the European Union and the UN Secretary-General objected, and the UN General Assembly later adopted a resolution declaring any decision altering Jerusalem's status null and void.

perspectives.framing: Presented the decision as recognition of reality, since Jerusalem is the seat of Israel's government, and as a step that would advance rather than hinder peace; the administration said it remained committed to a negotiated agreement.
Hailed recognition of Jerusalem as the eternal, undivided capital of the Jewish people and urged other states to follow.

Called the decision a violation of international law and UN resolutions that destroyed the US role as an honest broker, declared 'days of rage', and insisted East Jerusalem must be the capital of a Palestinian state.

The Secretary-General warned against unilateral measures that jeopardise a two-state solution; the General Assembly voted 128 to 9 on 21 December 2017 that the status of Jerusalem must be resolved through negotiations.

title: Great March of Return protests at the Gaza perimeter fence
summary: On 30 March 2018, Land Day, tens of thousands of Palestinians began weekly demonstrations along Gaza's perimeter fence, organised by a committee of civil-society groups and factions including Hamas, demanding the right of return of refugees and an end to the blockade. Most participants stayed in tent camps hundreds of metres from the fence; smaller groups approached it, burned tyres, threw stones and incendiary devices and at times tried to breach it. Israeli forces, including snipers, used live fire, and the IDF said it was defending the border against Hamas-orchestrated attacks. A UN Commission of Inquiry found that between 30 March and 31 December 2018 Israeli forces killed 189 Palestinians, including 35 children, and shot more than 6,100 with live ammunition; one Israeli soldier was killed in July 2018. The protests continued at declining intensity until December 2019, when organisers suspended them.

perspectives.framing: Described the marches as a peaceful popular movement asserting the right of return under UN resolution 194 and protesting the siege; Hamas embraced the protests as part of the resistance.

Called the events violent riots organised and financed by Hamas as cover for attacks and attempts to breach the fence and infiltrate Israeli communities, said its rules of engagement were lawful, and noted that Hamas acknowledged many of the dead as its members.

The Human Rights Council's Commission of Inquiry found reasonable grounds to believe Israeli snipers shot at protesters who posed no imminent threat, including children, journalists and medics, possibly amounting to crimes against humanity; OCHA documented mass casualties overwhelming Gaza's health system.

Amnesty International and B'Tselem said the use of lethal force against unarmed demonstrators was unlawful and called for an arms embargo, while also noting the throwing of incendiary devices by some protesters.

title: US embassy opens in Jerusalem; deadliest day of the Gaza protests
summary: On 14 May 2018, the 70th anniversary of Israel's declaration of independence, the United States formally opened its embassy in Jerusalem at its former consular building in the Arnona neighbourhood, with Ivanka Trump, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu among those attending the ceremony. The same day, tens of thousands of Palestinians joined Great March of Return demonstrations at the Gaza perimeter fence, timed to the eve of Nakba Day. Israeli forces fired on demonstrators approaching the fence. The Gaza Health Ministry reported at least 58 Palestinians killed and about 2,700 injured, the deadliest day in Gaza since the 2014 war, while the IDF said it was countering Hamas-directed attempts to breach the fence and later said many of the dead were Hamas members. The split-screen images drew international condemnation and a UN Human Rights Council inquiry.

Celebrated the embassy as a historic affirmation of Jerusalem's status and said its forces were defending the border against a Hamas-led assault, praising soldiers' restraint.
Abbas called the embassy an American 'settlement outpost' in Jerusalem, declared a day of mourning and a general strike, and accused Israel of massacres in Gaza.

The Secretary-General and human-rights officials expressed alarm at the loss of life and called for an independent investigation; the Human Rights Council voted days later to establish a commission of inquiry.

title: Knesset passes the Nation-State Basic Law
summary: On 19 July 2018, after an all-night debate, the Knesset passed Basic Law: Israel - the Nation-State of the Jewish People by 62 votes to 55 with two abstentions. The law, which has quasi-constitutional status, defines Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people in which the right to national self-determination is 'unique to the Jewish people', declares a 'complete and united' Jerusalem the capital, makes Hebrew the state language while granting Arabic 'special status', and states that the state views Jewish settlement as a national value to be encouraged. It contains no reference to equality. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called it a defining moment in the history of Zionism; Arab members of Knesset tore up copies in the chamber, and Adalah and other civil-rights groups said it entrenched discrimination against Arab citizens, a fifth of the population. The Supreme Court upheld the law in July 2021.

title: Abraham Accords: Israel normalises relations with the UAE and Bahrain
summary: On 15 September 2020, at a White House ceremony hosted by President Donald Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed normalisation agreements with the foreign ministers of the United Arab Emirates, Abdullah bin Zayed, and Bahrain, Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani, together with a joint Abraham Accords Declaration. They were the first Arab-Israeli peace agreements since Jordan's 1994 treaty and the first with Gulf states. The UAE agreement, announced on 13 August 2020, was tied to Israel suspending the annexation of parts of the West Bank envisaged under the Trump peace plan. Sudan and Morocco joined later in 2020. The Palestinian leadership condemned the accords as a betrayal of the Arab Peace Initiative's land-for-peace formula, and Iran and Turkey denounced them, while the signatories described a new era of regional cooperation in trade, security, tourism and technology.

perspectives.framing: Trump called the accords the dawn of a new Middle East and a historic breakthrough that bypassed the Palestinian veto over Arab-Israeli peace; the administration paired them with arms sales and other incentives.

Netanyahu described peace for peace rather than land for peace, presenting the accords as proof that normalisation need not wait for a Palestinian agreement, while stating that annexation was suspended, not cancelled.
Framed the agreements as a pragmatic choice for stability and prosperity, and credited the UAE deal with halting annexation and preserving the possibility of a Palestinian state.
Both condemned the accords as a stab in the back that rewarded occupation and abandoned the Arab consensus; the PA recalled its ambassadors from Abu Dhabi and Manama.

title: May 2021 Gaza war (Operation Guardian of the Walls)
summary: After weeks of tension in Jerusalem over threatened evictions in Sheikh Jarrah and clashes at the al-Aqsa compound on the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif, Hamas fired rockets toward Jerusalem on 10 May 2021 and Israel launched Operation Guardian of the Walls. Over 11 days Palestinian armed groups fired more than 4,000 rockets at Israel, and Israel carried out air strikes across Gaza, destroying several high-rise buildings, one housing media offices, and Hamas's tunnel network. According to the UN human rights office as cited by OCHA, 256 Palestinians were killed in Gaza, including 66 children and 40 women, of whom 128 were believed to be civilians, 62 members of armed groups and 66 undetermined; Israel said most of the dead were combatants. In Israel, 12 residents, including two children, and one soldier were killed. An Egyptian-brokered ceasefire took effect on 21 May 2021.

perspectives.framing: Described the operation as a response to unprovoked rocket fire on Jerusalem, said it struck Hamas's 'metro' tunnels and commanders with unprecedented precision, and attributed civilian deaths to Hamas's use of residential buildings and to rockets falling short inside Gaza.

Presented its rocket fire as the 'Sword of Jerusalem' in defence of al-Aqsa and Sheikh Jarrah, claimed victory for forcing Israel into a ceasefire and for linking Gaza to Jerusalem, and framed the fighting as resistance to occupation.

OCHA reported mass displacement and damage to homes, hospitals and water systems; the Secretary-General called for an immediate ceasefire, and the Human Rights Council established a standing commission of inquiry.
Brokered the ceasefire, pledged reconstruction funds and presented itself as the essential intermediary between Israel, Hamas and the Palestinian Authority.
Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International said certain Israeli strikes on residential buildings and Palestinian rocket attacks on Israeli towns appeared to violate the laws of war.

title: Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh killed in Jenin
summary: On 11 May 2022, Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American correspondent for Al Jazeera, was shot dead while covering an Israeli military raid at the entrance to the Jenin refugee camp in the northern West Bank; she was wearing a helmet and a press vest and a colleague was wounded. Israel initially suggested she might have been hit by Palestinian gunfire. In June 2022 the UN human rights office concluded that the fatal shot came from Israeli forces and that no warning had been issued and no shooting was taking place nearby; in July the United States assessed that Israeli fire was likely responsible but found no evidence of intent; and in September 2022 the IDF said there was a 'high possibility' that a soldier firing at gunmen had accidentally hit her, and that no criminal investigation would follow. Israeli police assaulted pallbearers at her Jerusalem funeral, drawing further international criticism.

perspectives.framing: Described the killing as a deliberate assassination of a journalist by Israeli forces, rejected joint investigation with Israel, and referred the case to the International Criminal Court.

Said soldiers were under heavy fire from Palestinian gunmen in Jenin, that Abu Akleh was not deliberately targeted, and that the incident was a tragic accident of combat for which no disciplinary action was warranted.

The human-rights office found the shots that killed her came from Israeli security forces and called for a criminal investigation; UN experts later said lethal force had been used without justification.

The State Department said forensic analysis was inconclusive but that fire from IDF positions was likely responsible, called the death a tragedy and urged accountability, while resisting congressional calls for an FBI inquiry.

title: Operation Breaking Dawn: Israel-Islamic Jihad fighting in Gaza
summary: On 5 August 2022, after arresting Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) leader Bassem al-Saadi in Jenin on 1 August and closing Gaza's crossings in anticipation of retaliation, Israel launched Operation Breaking Dawn with air strikes that killed Tayseer al-Jabari, commander of PIJ's forces in northern Gaza; a second commander, Khaled Mansour, was killed the following day. The Gaza Health Ministry reported 49 Palestinians killed, including 17 children; the IDF attributed several of those deaths, including children in Jabalia, to PIJ rockets that misfired inside Gaza. No Israelis were killed. An Egyptian-mediated ceasefire took effect at 23:30 on 7 August 2022, after which Gaza's crossings reopened.

perspectives.framing: Described a pre-emptive operation against an imminent PIJ anti-tank attack, targeting only Islamic Jihad while avoiding a wider war with Hamas, and emphasised that a large share of Palestinian deaths were caused by PIJ's own rockets.
Called the strikes an assassination campaign and a crime, vowed revenge for its commanders and framed its rocket fire as a unified resistance response; Iran praised the group's steadfastness.
Condemned Israel's aggression and expressed solidarity with PIJ but refrained from joining the fighting, prioritising the calm and economic measures reached after 2021.

The Special Coordinator urged de-escalation, expressed concern at civilian deaths including children, and welcomed Egypt's mediation; OCHA documented the impact of the crossing closures on fuel and electricity.

title: Huwara: two Israelis shot dead, settlers set the town ablaze
summary: On 26 February 2023, a Palestinian gunman shot dead two Israeli brothers from the settlement of Har Bracha, Hallel and Yagel Yaniv, as they drove through Huwara, a Palestinian town on Route 60 south of Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. That evening hundreds of Israeli settlers entered Huwara and neighbouring villages, setting fire to homes, cars and businesses. Palestinian officials reported one man, Sameh Aqtash, shot dead in nearby Za'tara and around 100 people injured, with dozens of homes and vehicles burned. The IDF's regional commander later described the rampage as a 'pogrom', and video evidence indicated that soldiers present did little to stop it. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said Huwara should be 'wiped out' by the state, remarks he walked back after condemnation from the United States and others. The events came hours after Israeli and Palestinian officials pledged de-escalation at a summit in Aqaba, Jordan.

perspectives.framing: Condemned the killing of the Yaniv brothers as a terrorist attack, called on citizens not to take the law into their own hands, and said the army would pursue both the gunman and the arsonists; Smotrich and other coalition members blamed Palestinian terror for the settlers' anger.
Described the settler attack as a state-backed pogrom carried out under army protection and evidence of the government's annexationist agenda, and suspended engagement with the Aqaba process.
Hailed the shooting as a heroic operation and a response to Israeli raids, and later confirmed the gunman, killed by Israeli forces in March, as a member.
Condemned both the shooting and the settler violence, called Smotrich's remarks repugnant and disgusting, and pressed Israel to prosecute those responsible for the rampage.

title: Israeli military operation in the Jenin refugee camp
summary: From the early hours of 3 July 2023, Israel conducted its largest military operation in the West Bank in nearly two decades, sending about 1,000 troops with drone strikes and armoured bulldozers into the Jenin refugee camp, which the IDF described as a stronghold of the armed 'Jenin Brigades' responsible for attacks on Israelis. Troops withdrew overnight on 4-5 July. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, 12 Palestinians, including four children, were killed and 143 injured; the IDF said all those killed were combatants and reported one soldier killed. UN OCHA reported that thousands of camp residents were temporarily displaced and that roads, water and electricity networks were extensively damaged. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas suspended security coordination with Israel, the UN Secretary-General voiced concern at the use of air strikes in the densely populated camp, and Israel said the operation targeted militants and their weapons.

perspectives.framing: Called it a counter-terrorism operation, not a war, against a Jenin-based network responsible for dozens of shooting attacks and sheltered by Iran-backed groups, said it was carried out with precision and that all the dead were combatants, and said the army would return whenever necessary.
Described the operation as a war crime and a new Nakba against the camp, suspended security coordination, and called on the UN Security Council to act.
Praised the camp's fighters as heroes of resistance, claimed the operation had failed, and framed the events as part of a wider struggle against occupation.

The Secretary-General said air strikes were inconsistent with law-enforcement standards and expressed concern for civilians; OCHA and UNRWA documented displacement, damaged infrastructure and obstructed medical access.

title: Hamas-led attack on southern Israel
summary: At dawn on 7 October 2023, during the Simchat Torah holiday, Hamas-led militants fired thousands of rockets and breached the Gaza perimeter fence at dozens of points, attacking army bases, kibbutzim, the town of Sderot and the Nova music festival near Re'im. According to the Israeli government, about 1,200 people were killed, most of them civilians, and 251 people were taken hostage into Gaza; the IDF said it killed roughly 1,000 attackers inside Israel over the following days. It was the deadliest single day for Israel since its founding. Israeli air strikes on Gaza began the same day; the Gaza Health Ministry reported 232 Palestinians killed in Gaza on 7 October. Israel's government declared a state of war the next morning and mobilised reservists, opening the Gaza war that dominates this era.

perspectives.framing: Describes 7 October as a massacre and the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust, a 'terrorist' assault on civilians that justified a war to destroy Hamas and recover the hostages; Israel names its campaign Operation Swords of Iron.

Calls the assault 'Operation Al-Aqsa Flood', presenting it as a legitimate act of resistance against occupation and blockade and a response to Israeli actions at Al-Aqsa Mosque and against prisoners; it disputes that fighters deliberately targeted civilians.

Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attacks and hostage-taking as unjustifiable while saying they 'did not happen in a vacuum', pointing to decades of occupation; the UN Commission of Inquiry later found war crimes committed by Palestinian armed groups on 7 October.
President Biden called the attack 'pure, unadulterated evil' and 'sheer evil', affirmed Israel's right to defend itself and sent naval forces to the region as a deterrent.

title: Hezbollah opens a northern front against Israel
summary: On 8 October 2023 Hezbollah fired rockets and guided missiles at Israeli positions in the Shebaa Farms area, which Lebanon claims and Israel occupies, declaring it was acting 'in solidarity' with the Palestinian people. Israel responded with artillery and air strikes in southern Lebanon. The exchanges settled into a daily pattern of cross-border fire that Hezbollah described as a 'support front' calibrated to avoid full-scale war, while the IDF struck launch teams and commanders, killing hundreds of Hezbollah fighters over the following months according to IDF and Hezbollah announcements. Israel evacuated more than 60,000 residents from communities near the border, per the Israeli government, and the UN's migration agency estimated that roughly 90,000 people were displaced from southern Lebanon by early 2024. The front remained limited until the escalation of September 2024.
