title: Israel declares war and launches air campaign on Gaza
summary: On 8 October 2023 Israel's security cabinet formally declared a state of war under Article 40 of Basic Law: The Government, the first such declaration since 1973, and the IDF said it was mobilising some 300,000 reservists. Air strikes on the Gaza Strip, which had begun on 7 October, expanded into a sustained bombing campaign against what the IDF described as Hamas command centres, tunnels, rocket sites and the homes of operatives across Gaza City and the north. On 9 October Defence Minister Yoav Gallant ordered a 'complete siege', cutting electricity, fuel, food and water supplies from Israel. By the evening of 8 October the Gaza Health Ministry reported 370 Palestinians killed and 1,788 injured since the war began, figures that rose by hundreds daily during the following weeks.

perspectives.framing: Frames the campaign as a defensive war of necessity against a 'terror army' embedded in civilian areas, with the stated aims of dismantling Hamas's military and governing capacity and returning the hostages; the siege was justified as lawful pressure on a 'terrorist' entity.

Portrays the strikes as indiscriminate 'aggression' and collective punishment of a besieged population, and the siege as a war crime; it vowed to keep fighting and to trade hostages for Palestinian prisoners.

OCHA and the Secretary-General warned that a total siege violated international humanitarian law, called for humanitarian access and urged all parties to protect civilians, while UN human-rights bodies criticised the scale of strikes on residential areas.
Warned against any displacement of Gazans into Sinai, called for restraint and for the opening of the Rafah crossing to aid, positioning itself as mediator.

title: Mass internal displacement across the Gaza Strip
summary: On 13 October 2023 the IDF ordered the roughly 1.1 million residents of Gaza north of Wadi Gaza to move south within 24 hours ahead of its ground offensive, an order the UN said could not be carried out without devastating humanitarian consequences. Hundreds of thousands crowded into UNRWA schools, hospitals and tent camps in the centre and south, and were displaced again by the Khan Younis offensive in December and the Rafah offensive in May 2024. UN OCHA estimated that about 1.9 million people, roughly nine in ten Gazans, had been internally displaced by mid-2024, many of them several times, and that by August 2024 IDF evacuation orders covered more than 80 per cent of the Strip. On the Israeli side, the government evacuated tens of thousands of residents from communities near Gaza and the Lebanese border.

perspectives.framing: Describes evacuation orders as measures to move civilians out of combat zones and away from Hamas positions, and designates 'humanitarian zones' such as al-Mawasi; it accuses Hamas of preventing civilians from leaving and of using them as human shields.
Together with Hamas, describes the displacement as a 'second Nakba' (the 1948 Palestinian displacement) and forced transfer aimed at emptying Gaza, and rejects any resettlement outside the territory.

OCHA and UNRWA call it the largest displacement of Palestinians since 1948, say no place in Gaza is safe, and report that shelters are overcrowded and repeatedly hit; UN officials warned that mass evacuation orders are incompatible with international humanitarian law when no safe destination exists.
Rejected any transfer of Gazans into Sinai as a liquidation of the Palestinian cause and a security threat, and kept the Rafah crossing open only for limited aid and evacuations.

The event triggered protests across the Arab world and the cancellation of a planned summit with President Biden in Amman.

title: Israel launches ground invasion of northern Gaza

title: IDF raids Al-Shifa Hospital

title: Week-long truce and hostage-prisoner exchanges
summary: A truce brokered by Qatar, Egypt and the United States took effect on 24 November 2023, the first pause in fighting since 7 October. title: Israeli offensive in Khan Younis

title: Deaths at aid convoy in Gaza City ('flour massacre')
summary: Before dawn on 29 February 2024, crowds of thousands converged on a convoy of trucks carrying flour along the coastal al-Rashid road near the Nabulsi roundabout in southwestern Gaza City, an area where the UN had warned of imminent famine. The Secretary-General condemned the incident, OHCHR said it had verified deaths from gunfire and demanded an effective investigation, and OCHA stressed the collapse of orderly aid distribution in the north.

title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 2728 demanding a ceasefire
summary: On 25 March 2024 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2728 by 14 votes to none, with the United States abstaining, after three earlier ceasefire drafts had been vetoed by the United States or by Russia and China. The resolution demanded an immediate ceasefire for the month of Ramadan leading to a lasting and sustainable ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, and the lifting of barriers to humanitarian assistance at scale. It was the Council's first ceasefire demand of the war, following resolutions 2712 and 2720 on humanitarian pauses and aid. The US abstention marked a public rift with Israel, whose prime minister cancelled a planned delegation to Washington in protest. Fighting continued and the parties disagreed over whether the resolution was binding; the Gaza Health Ministry's toll passed 32,000 that week.

perspectives.framing: The Secretary-General said the resolution must be implemented and that failure would be unforgivable; most Council members and the UN Secretariat treated it as binding on the parties.

Welcomed the demand for a ceasefire, said it was ready for an immediate exchange of prisoners and hostages and accused Israel of defying the Council.

Explained its abstention by saying it supported the goals but objected to the absence of a condemnation of Hamas, and characterised the resolution as non-binding, a position contested by other members.

title: ICJ advisory opinion finds Israel's occupation unlawful
summary: On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice delivered an advisory opinion requested by the UN General Assembly in December 2022 on the legal consequences of Israel's policies and practices in the occupied Palestinian territory. By 11 votes to 4 the court found that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza is unlawful, that Israel is obliged to end it as rapidly as possible, cease settlement activity, evacuate settlers and make reparation, and that other states must not recognise or assist the situation. It also found that Israel's policies breached the prohibition of racial segregation and apartheid under Article 3 of the CERD convention, without adjudicating which term applied. Although non-binding, the opinion was the court's most sweeping statement on the occupation; the General Assembly in September 2024 adopted a resolution demanding that Israel end its presence within twelve months.

Said it was concerned by the breadth of the opinion, argued it would complicate efforts toward a negotiated two-state solution and rejected the idea that the court could compel a unilateral withdrawal.

title: Pager and radio explosions strike Hezbollah members across Lebanon

title: Israeli airstrike kills Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in Beirut

title: Knesset passes laws banning UNRWA activity in Israel

title: ICC issues arrest warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant and Deif
summary: On 21 November 2024 a pre-trial chamber of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, former defence minister Yoav Gallant and Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif, finding reasonable grounds to believe each bore criminal responsibility for war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza war; Israel said it had killed Deif in July. title: Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire takes effect in Lebanon
summary: A US- and French-brokered cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah took effect at 04:00 on 27 November 2024, ending more than 13 months of cross-border conflict that had escalated into full-scale war in September. Said any Israeli presence was an occupation that the Lebanese state must end by all means, while stopping short of resuming attacks.

The Special Coordinator and UNIFIL commander jointly urged both parties to meet their obligations so that safety could be restored to communities on both sides of the Blue Line, and reported continuing Lebanese army deployment.

title: Israel halts entry of all goods and aid into Gaza
summary: On 2 March 2025, the day after the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire expired, Israel announced that it was halting the entry of all goods and humanitarian supplies into the Gaza Strip until Hamas accepted a US proposal to extend the first phase and release more hostages, rather than proceeding to the second phase. The Kerem Shalom, Erez and Zikim crossings were closed to cargo, leaving thousands of tents and other supplies undelivered, according to the UN, which said aid had reached nearly every person in Gaza during the preceding six weeks. The UN emergency relief coordinator called the decision alarming and said international humanitarian law required access for life-saving aid; Egypt, Qatar and other Arab states condemned the move, while Israel said it was lawful pressure on Hamas and denied using food as a weapon. The blockade lasted about eleven weeks, until limited deliveries resumed in late May, and preceded the collapse of the ceasefire on 18 March.

perspectives.framing: Said Hamas had refused the US 'Witkoff' extension framework, that enough aid had entered during phase one to last for months, that Hamas was diverting supplies, and that halting entry was legitimate leverage rather than a weapon against civilians.
Called the halt a war crime and 'cheap blackmail', accused Israel of violating the ceasefire, and demanded implementation of the second phase as agreed.
Condemned the use of humanitarian aid as a bargaining tool and said there was no alternative to the original agreement.

The Secretary-General urged all parties to prevent a return to hostilities and called for aid to flow immediately; the emergency relief coordinator called Israel's decision alarming and said international humanitarian law is clear that access must be allowed.

title: US air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen
summary: On 15 March 2025 the United States began large-scale air and naval strikes on Houthi targets across Yemen, which President Donald Trump said would use 'overwhelming lethal force' until the Iran-aligned movement stopped attacking Red Sea shipping; the Houthis had announced a resumption of attacks on Israeli-linked ships in response to Israel's halt of aid to Gaza. The Houthi-run health ministry reported at least 31 people killed and more than 100 injured in the first day of strikes, according to Al Jazeera, and the Houthis vowed to respond, continuing missile and drone launches at Israel and at US warships. The campaign, which included strikes on ports and on Sanaa, ended on 6 May when Trump announced that the Houthis had agreed to stop attacking US vessels in an Oman-brokered understanding that did not cover Israel; Israel separately struck Sanaa airport and the port of Hodeidah after a Houthi missile hit near Ben Gurion Airport.

perspectives.framing: Framed the campaign as restoring freedom of navigation and deterring Iran's proxy, warned Tehran that it would be held responsible for Houthi attacks, and later presented the Oman-brokered halt as the Houthis 'capitulating'.

Described the strikes as US-Israeli aggression and war crimes against Yemeni civilians, said its blockade was in solidarity with Gaza and would continue against Israel, and claimed to have forced the United States to stop.
Denied directing the Houthis, condemned the US strikes as a violation of Yemen's sovereignty and the UN Charter, and warned it would respond decisively to any attack on Iran.
Welcomed US action against a 'terrorist' proxy but stressed that Israel would act alone against Houthi attacks on its territory, striking Yemeni ports and airport infrastructure.

title: Israeli strikes across Gaza end the two-month ceasefire
summary: In the early hours of 18 March 2025 Israel launched waves of air strikes across the Gaza Strip, ending the ceasefire that had held since 19 January. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said he had ordered the strikes after Hamas refused proposals to extend the first phase and release more hostages, and Israel said it targeted Hamas commanders and infrastructure. Gaza's health ministry recorded 436 people killed on 18 March, and Western newspapers reported more than 400 dead, among the highest single-day tolls of the war; the ministry's cumulative count passed 50,000 on 23 March, while no independent or Israeli total was available. A UN staff member was killed and five injured when UN guesthouses in Deir al-Balah were hit on 19 March. Israel resumed ground operations on 20 March, re-entering the Netzarim area and northern Gaza. The UN Secretary-General said he was shocked and appealed for the ceasefire to be restored, aid to resume and hostages to be released.

perspectives.framing: Said the strikes were a response to Hamas's refusal to release hostages and its rearming during the truce, that they targeted Hamas commanders and terrorist infrastructure, and that fighting would continue with increasing force until all hostages were returned.
Accused Israel of unilaterally overturning the agreement, called the strikes 'massacres' against sleeping civilians during Ramadan, and blamed the United States for enabling the return to war.
The Trump administration said it had been consulted, blamed Hamas for rejecting extension proposals, and backed Israel's decision.

The Secretary-General expressed shock at the strikes and hundreds of reported deaths, appealed for the ceasefire to be respected, and condemned the strike on UN premises that killed a UNOPS staff member.

title: Houthi ballistic missile strikes near Ben Gurion Airport
summary: On the morning of 4 May 2025 a ballistic missile launched from Yemen by the Houthi movement evaded Israeli and US interceptors and struck an access road beside Terminal 3 of Ben Gurion Airport, Israel's main international gateway, leaving a large crater. Israeli emergency services reported four people lightly injured, and flights were suspended for about an hour, after which many foreign airlines cancelled services to Israel for days or weeks. The Houthis said the strike was in support of Gaza and announced an 'aerial blockade' of Israel; Israel promised retaliation and on 5 and 6 May struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah and Sanaa international airport, which the Israeli military said it had disabled. The attack came as Israel's security cabinet approved plans to expand the Gaza offensive and call up tens of thousands of reservists. Two days later the United States announced a separate ceasefire with the Houthis that did not include Israel.

perspectives.framing: Claimed a successful hypersonic strike on the 'Zionist entity's' main airport in support of Gaza, declared an air blockade on Israel and urged airlines to stay away.

Called the strike an Iranian-backed terrorist attack that air defences had failed to stop, vowed a sevenfold response, and struck Houthi-controlled ports and Sanaa airport, warning that Iran was responsible for its proxy.
Continued its own campaign against the Houthis but days later announced an Oman-brokered halt covering US ships, saying the Houthis had agreed not to attack American vessels.

title: Operation Gideon's Chariots: Israel launches expanded Gaza offensive
summary: On 16 and 17 May 2025 the Israel Defense Forces launched 'Gideon's Chariots', an expanded ground and air offensive intended, in the government's words, to seize and hold 'strategic areas' of the Gaza Strip, defeat Hamas and pressure it to release the remaining 58 hostages, following a security cabinet decision earlier in the month to conquer territory and move the population southward. Heavy strikes preceded the ground advance: the Guardian reported more than 140 Palestinians killed in 24 hours and Gaza rescuers told the BBC at least 300 had been killed since 15 May. Gaza's health ministry counted 53,272 people killed since October 2023 as of 17 May; the BBC noted the ministry does not distinguish combatants and that Israel disputes its breakdown. Talks resumed in Doha the same day, and on 26 May Israel issued a displacement order covering about 40 per cent of the Strip, according to UN OCHA. The offensive continued beyond June 2025.

perspectives.framing: Described a decisive operation to achieve all war aims, defeat Hamas, seize and hold territory, separate civilians from Hamas by moving them to 'humanitarian zones' in the south, and bring the hostages home, while announcing limited aid entry to avert famine.

Called the offensive a campaign of extermination and forced displacement, said no hostages would be released without an end to the war and full withdrawal, and offered partial releases for a 60-day truce.

OCHA reported that air and ground operations were dismantling the means of survival for 2.1 million people, that displacement orders now covered over 40 per cent of the Strip, and that the entire population faced the risk of famine.

Britain, France, Canada and others condemned the expansion and aid restrictions as 'egregious', Arab League states meeting in Baghdad called for an immediate ceasefire, and some governments used the term 'ethnic cleansing'.

title: Gaza Humanitarian Foundation begins aid distribution; deaths near aid sites
summary: On 27 May 2025 the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), a US- and Israeli-backed private mechanism guarded by American security contractors and the Israeli military, began distributing food from a site near Rafah, replacing UN-led distribution that Israel said Hamas had diverted. Crowds overran the site on the first day, and the UN reported dozens shot and injured trying to reach supplies; the UN and major aid agencies refused to take part, calling the model 'engineered scarcity' that forced civilians through militarised zones. Reports of Palestinians killed by gunfire while approaching the sites followed: on 1 June medics reported at least 15 dead and Gaza health officials more than 30 near the Rafah site, while the Israeli military said troops fired warning shots and GHF disputed accounts of shootings at its sites. Gaza's health ministry counted 516 aid seekers killed by 24 June, and the UN human rights office later said hundreds had been killed around the sites.

perspectives.framing: Presented the foundation as a way to feed Gazans while preventing Hamas from looting and profiting from aid, said millions of meals were distributed, denied that its sites were scenes of shootings, and said troops fired warning shots at individuals who approached them in a threatening manner.
Backed and later funded GHF as an innovative solution, blamed Hamas for violence near the sites and criticised the UN for refusing to cooperate.

Called the scheme a militarised distraction from the UN's principled plan, said it forced starving people to walk through combat zones and could not meet needs, and the Secretary-General condemned the reported killings of people seeking aid as unacceptable.
Called the sites 'death traps' and 'humiliation', accused Israel of using hunger as a weapon, and published daily tallies of aid seekers killed.

title: Israel–Iran war: twelve days of strikes end in a US-announced ceasefire
summary: Before dawn on 13 June 2025 Israel launched 'Operation Rising Lion', strikes across Iran that hit the Natanz enrichment site, missile bases and residential compounds, killing Revolutionary Guard commander Hossein Salami, armed forces chief Mohammad Bagheri and at least nine nuclear scientists, according to Israeli and Iranian statements. Iran responded with waves of ballistic missiles and drones at Israeli cities. The United States joined on 22 June with strikes on three nuclear sites, and Iran fired missiles at the US Al Udeid base in Qatar on 23 June. A ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump took effect on 24 June after a final Iranian strike killed four people in Beersheba. Iran's health ministry recorded 627 people killed and nearly 5,000 injured, per the BBC; Israeli authorities reported 28 killed and more than 3,000 wounded from about 550 missiles and 1,000 drones, per The Times of Israel. The UN Secretary-General condemned the escalation and urged both sides to respect the ceasefire.

perspectives.framing: Called the campaign a pre-emptive operation against an existential nuclear and missile threat, said it had set Iran's nuclear programme back years and degraded its missile forces, and declared its goals achieved.

Denounced the strikes as an unprovoked act of war and 'aggression' by the 'Zionist regime' and the United States during nuclear talks, framed its missile barrages as legitimate self-defence, and claimed victory in an 'imposed war'.
President Trump backed Israel, struck Iran's nuclear sites, then brokered and announced the ceasefire, calling it the end of the '12 Day War' and pressing both sides not to violate it.

The Secretary-General condemned military escalation, was particularly concerned by attacks on nuclear installations while US-Iran talks were under way, called for maximum restraint, and welcomed the ceasefire.

title: United States strikes Iranian nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan
summary: In the early hours of 22 June 2025 (Iran time) the United States entered the Israel–Iran war directly: B-2 stealth bombers dropped bunker-busting bombs on the deeply buried Fordow enrichment plant and on Natanz, while submarine-launched cruise missiles struck facilities at Isfahan, in an operation the Pentagon called 'Midnight Hammer'. President Donald Trump declared the sites 'obliterated' and warned Iran against retaliation; Iranian officials condemned the attack, asserted a right to self-defence, and Iran's parliament later voted to suspend cooperation with the IAEA. The IAEA reported major destruction at Natanz and Isfahan but said the extent of damage at Fordow and the whereabouts of Iran's enriched uranium were unclear, and US officials and outside experts disputed how far the programme had been set back. The UN Secretary-General told the Security Council the bombing marked 'a perilous turn'. Iran retaliated the next day with missiles at Al Udeid air base in Qatar, before a ceasefire took effect on 24 June.

perspectives.framing: Described a spectacular, one-off success that obliterated Iran's key enrichment sites, removed a nuclear threat and created the conditions for peace, while insisting it did not seek regime change or a wider war.

Called the strikes a flagrant violation of the UN Charter, the NPT and IAEA safeguards, reserved 'all options' for self-defence, and struck the US base in Qatar in a telegraphed response; parliament moved to suspend IAEA cooperation.
Praised the strikes as a historic decision that completed its own campaign against Iran's nuclear programme.

The Secretary-General warned of a 'rathole of retaliation' and said Iran must respect the NPT while all states must act within the Charter; the IAEA reported severe damage but could not verify the fate of enriched uranium and called for inspectors' access.
